speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF COMMONWEALTH TECHNICAL TRAINING WEEK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with leave of the house I should like to make a statement on commonwealth technical training week, which begins today. The idea of holding a special week to focus attention on the importance of education and training, particularly the technical form of training, originated with His Royal Highness the Duke of Edinburgh. This week is being observed simultaneously in Great Britain and many other countries of the commonwealth.
As a first step in arranging for this week, I consulted with the premiers of the provinces, and early this year I called a meeting in Ottawa which was attended by representatives of the federal and provincial governments, labour, management, and a number of national organizations. The idea received complete endorsement.
At the national meeting, five broad objectives for a commonwealth technical training week were adopted. The first is to try to create more public awareness of the excellent career opportunities which exist in the technical and vocational fields. There is still, among an ever decreasing minority, I am glad to say, a tendency in this country to think of the "white collar" occupations as being more desirable, even though many of them demand less education and training than do many of the skilled and technical jobs. We must give the technical and vocational careers their proper place of importance.
The second objective is to stimulate more apprenticeship and other in-plant training programs. There are not enough programs of this kind now in existence, although where they are they have proved their worth both in Canada and other countries.
The third objective is to convince young people of the necessity of planning a career and of staying in school until graduation, seeking training which will fit them for the modern demands of advanced technology. Present rates of drop-outs from school reveal that 70 per cent of students entering grade 11 of elementary school will have left before 90205-6-347i
they get their junior matriculation. This is a serious matter when viewed in relation to the widespread reduction, since world war II, of unskilled and semi-skilled occupations through the introduction of more and better machines and more efficient methods.
The fourth objective is to encourage adults to upgrade their skills and increase their education, and to stimulate the establishment of more adult education and training programs. There is a reluctance on the part of adults to take advantage of available facilities, as illustrated by the fact that less than 5 per cent of unemployed persons apply for the training in programs operated in a number of the provinces.
The fifth objective of the week is to bring together industry and the schools so there can be a greater understanding of each other's needs. The rapidly changing patten of employment and occupations makes it essential that industry and the schools develop closer co-operation so that more courses can be vocationally oriented.
All these broad objectives, I realize, cannot be reached during one short week; but if public attention is drawn to them, and more people in positions of leadership at all levels, national, provincial and municipal, become aware of the need for positive planning and action to reach these objectives, then this commonwealth technical training week will have been worth while.
It was agreed at the federal-provincial planning meeting that each province would organize the observance of the week within its own jurisdiction. The federal government will provide assistance in the way of pamphlets and posters for the schools, along with film material for the schools and television, as well as generally assisting in organizing some national publicity for the objectives of the week.
All these plans give full respect to the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces in respect to education. This has been worked out, and each province has organized a variety of methods for bringing attention to the objectives of the week. Special pamphlets are being distributed through the secondary schools to each student to point out the need for young people remaining in school to get as much education and training as possible before seeking their first job. It is expected that the fundamental message, namely the need of action will be carried to young

Vocational Training
people and their parents. Through the cooperation of press, radio and television, I hope the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of the C.C.F. will join me in approval of what is being done and what is being attempted this week not only in our own country but in the United Kingdom and in various countries of the commonwealth.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF COMMONWEALTH TECHNICAL TRAINING WEEK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side are very happy to associate ourselves with the Prime Minister in what he has just said about the value of commonwealth technical training week. The importance of that week and the steps taken to publicize it in Canada have been made clear in a memorandum from the Minister of Labour, which I have before me, and by what the Prime Minister himself has said this morning. Also we can join the Prime Minister and others in expressing appreciation to the Duke of Edinburgh for the initiative he has taken in bringing about this important development.
It is a cliche, of course, Mr. Speaker, to say that we live in a technical and scientific age, but it is something that is very true, so it is necessary for technical education to keep abreast of the fantastic changes that have taken place both nationally and internationally. Perhaps it is also important to point out that while technical education is now more important than ever, and it is well for the federal government to associate with and assist the provinces in the development of technical education in every appropriate way, we can emphasize the importance of technical education without minimizing the importance of education in the humanities and in the social sciences; because it is also true that if we do not learn how to use for constructive purposes the machines we create, technical education itself may not be of any great value. The necessity for reconciliation of the two kinds of education was put in a striking way the other day by the head of the Carnegie Corporation in the United States when he said:
We must have respect for both our plumbers and our philosophers, or neither our pipes nor our theories will hold water.
Commonwealth technical education week also reminds us that progress in such education has been uneven within the commonwealth. Therefore, those members, including Canada, which have been more fortunate in their development in this field can help and are helping other members of the commonwealth to make similar progress. This is a kind of mutual aid which can underline the meaningful character of the commonwealth

association. In short, for domestic, commonwealth and international purposes it is important to give all the support we can to commonwealth technical training week. We on this side will be glad to support in any way we can the initiative and the work done by the government in this field.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF COMMONWEALTH TECHNICAL TRAINING WEEK
speechtext:
I am pleased on behalf of this group to associate myself with the words of the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in giving support to the commonwealth technical training week. I think we are becoming more and more aware of the fact that educational facilities require continuing change, and that the present unemployment situation and some of the things that have been learned from it demonstrate the great need at this time for increased skills for many of those who are out of work at the present time and require such training.
We are pleased that this is a commonwealth venture. We need such facilities and emphasis on such facilities in Canada, and they are also needed much more in other parts of the world. There is a challenge to the west today. There is a challenge to our educational system. Coupled with further improvements, we think this is a very good step to underline the need for further emphasis on technical training in Canada and in the other commonwealth nations.

Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that on March 15, when I announced some diplomatic appointments, I expressed the hope that Canada would shortly be able to open diplomatic relations with the Sudan as part of a program of strengthening Canadian representation in Asia and Africa.
I am pleased to announce that the government of the Sudan has agreed to accept a Canadian ambassador even though the Sudan government will not itself immediately be able to accredit an ambassador to Ottawa. Mr. R. A. D. Ford, who recently took up his appointment as Canadian ambassador to the United Arab Republic, will be concurrently accredited to the government of the Sudan.
The Sudan has close ties with both the Arab world and Africa south of the Sahara, and is becoming increasingly important in the United Nations. The appointment of a Canadian ambassador to that country reflects the importance which the Canadian government attaches to developments in Africa, and will encourage closer relations with one of that continent's most important countries.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to move the adjournment of the
Air Lines Labour Dispute house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the decision by Trans-Canada Air Lines to disregard the safety and well-being of its passengers by taking action to replace its present stewardesses, hostesses and pursers with other personnel who will not be required to undergo medical or physical examination and who will be accepted from any large group regardless of whether or not they qualify as flight attendants.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES LABOUR DISPUTE    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member can tell me when the decision to which he refers was taken, or whether it has been taken.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES LABOUR DISPUTE    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Yes. The decision referred to, and which just came to my attention over the week end, was taken by way of a teletype directive to all T.C.A. stations, sent by Mr. H. W. Seagrim, the vice president, on May 17, the day before a conciliation board report on this matter was released by the Minister of Labour; and this recruitment of personnel along the line suggested in the motion is currently taking place.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES LABOUR DISPUTE    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this dispute is under collective bargaining procedures and meetings were held last Thursday and Friday. I have no word that they have been discontinued. I feel that any motion such as this would have an effect on the discussions that are at present under way.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES LABOUR DISPUTE    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The definite matter of urgent public importance which the hon. member for Skeena wishes to have discussed under standing order 26, which involves the interruption of the normal course of business in order to discuss the matter, relates to a labour dispute between Trans-Canada Air Lines and some of its personnel, namely stewardesses, hostesses and pursers. It is put forward by the hon. member as a matter of the safety of passengers.
There are two aspects to the matter. One is the labour dispute, which undoubtedly is an important matter, as is that of the safety of passengers who travel by Trans-Canada Air Lines. The whole administration has been given to Trans-Canada Air Lines by parliament, and the management has the responsibility of continuing labour negotiations and assuring the safety of passengers.
It has been suggested that the decision interposes a matter of such urgency for debate that we should interrupt our proceedings. In view of the fact that this is a continuing labour dispute which, in so far as it is a matter of administrative responsibility, comes under the Department of Transport whose

Air Lines Labour Dispute estimates have been before the house in the last 10 days-in fact as recently as last week, I believe-and will be before the house again, as I am advised that the first item has not yet been passed, it seems to me that unless the matter is of immediate urgency for discussion-that is, that it must be discussed today or within a day or two-urgency of debate does not arise.
Furthermore, I think we would be abusing the rule if we projected labour disputes into our discussions every time there was a difference of opinion in an important section of labour relations in the country. Those are not unusual in occurrence. If we invoked the rule for this kind of thing I think we might have to change the rule, because we would be talking about little else.
As to the other aspect, that of safety, in view of the record of administration I think it will bear waiting until the hon. member can raise the item on the estimates. Therefore, with all respect to the hon. member, I do not think we have here a matter that should be allowed to intervene under standing order 26.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question arising out of a press report that Canadian flour milling companies with United States affiliations have been forbidden to bid on contracts for the export of flour to China.
In view of the answer given by the Minister of Agriculture on Saturday last, that the question of permits being granted by the United States to such companies is no concern of ours, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether it is not the policy of the Canadian government that all corporations operating in Canada should follow Canadian policy and should operate in the best economic interests of this country, and whether or not he feels it is an impingement on our sovereignty if these companies-as it is claimed in the report-are forbidden to export flour to China.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPORTED U.S. ACTION RESPECTING BIDS ON SALE TO CHINA
speechtext: Order. I do not know whether the Prime Minister can deal with the matter without notice, and I of course do not wish to intervene, but the hon. member's question is largely hypothetical. He does not take responsibility for the report, he indicates that he does not know whether the point arises at all, and then asks a rather indefinite question.

subtopic: REPORTED U.S. ACTION RESPECTING BIDS ON SALE TO CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the point of order, I think the accuracy of this has been rather well established by the answer from the Minister of Agriculture last Saturday, that the question of companies operating in Canada obtaining permits from the United States government is no concern of ours.
My question to the Prime Minister is this. Is it not the well known policy of the Canadian government that corporations operating in Canada should follow Canadian policy and should not have to go to the United States for permits to carry on export business with a country to which Canada is selling? I think the question is very much in order, and I thought the government had a policy on it.

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while I have no claim to being a linguist, I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) to a possible interpretation of the French translation of section 1 of Bill C-92. The English expression seems to cover the primary purpose of this piece of legislation.
More than ever, in considering this bill, we must face the two essential conditions of a crime. There must first be the actus reus, which is clearly determined in this case, and also the mens rea.
It seems to me that if we added the word "prepare" to paragraph (a) of subsection 2, we would have an exact translation of what the government and the Minister of Justice had in mind in introducing this bill. Thus the paragraph would read as follows:
Le meurtre est dit qualifie, h regard de toute personne, lorsqu'il est prepare, pro] etc et deli be re de la part de cette personne.
I do think the French translation would then be more complete and would not lend itself to any discussion. In my humble view, the intention of the legislators would also be much better expressed.

I wanted to make these few remarks to the Minister of Justice, as the matter was brought to my attention over the week end when I had the privilege of discussing this bill with members of the legal profession in Three Rivers.
I shall not belabour the point, but I think the French version should be more complete so as to convey the meaning of the English word "planned", which reflects the idea that the government had in mind in introducing this bill.

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the house passed on the principle of Bill C-92 when the motion for second reading was put.
As far as I am concerned, I will try to suggest various means of improving it so that it may meet as much as possible the expectations of the public on this important question of capital punishment.
Section 1 introduces a new section into the Criminal Code, section 202A, which does not change the definition of murder itself found under sections 201 and 202; it merely distinguishes between two categories of murder, capital and non-capital, depending on whether the crime is premeditated or not. Section 202A is therefore the key to the whole bill.
When I spoke on second reading of the bill, I stated that even if such a distinction could be justified in principle, in the general context of the bill it necessarily leads to what is practically the complete abolition of capital punishment. Now, not only the hon. members of this house but a vast majority of the citizens of this country wish to keep capital punishment in our statute books, not as a museum curiosity but as a necessary and efficient deterrent for the protection of honest people.
May I say first of all that by establishing two categories of murder, section 1 is contrary to the recommendations of one of the most important joint committees of the house and Senate. I will now repeat what I said the other day as reported on page 5227 of Hansard for May 23, 1961:
Several witnesses suggested that consideration might be given to the creation of degrees of murder which would take into account the difference in moral culpability between different types of homicides. All witnesses representing law-enforcement authorities opposed the establishment of degrees of murder. The committee shares the conclusions of the United Kingdom royal commission on this question. The committee is of the opinion that the present distinction between murder and manslaughter is quite clear and straightforward. It considers that any attempt to break murder down into degrees may lead to the creation of technical and confusing distinctions without, at the same time, creating any precise delineation between murders of differing degrees of moral culpability.
90205-6-348J
Criminal Code
Moreover, by proceeding as we are asked to do under section 1, we also depart from the legislation passed in the United Kingdom in 1957, which is known as the homicide act, 1957. Indeed, as seen on page 5221 of Hansard for May 23 last, the minister said with regard to that act:
In 1957 after further consideration the parliament of Great Britain passed an act entitled "The Homicide Act, 1957". This act adopted the approach of dividing murder into two classes, those which carry the death penalty and those for which the penalty is life imprisonment. The division, however, is based rather on the method or weapon by which the killing is accomplished, or in certain cases upon the person or class of person killed rather than on the nature and circmustances of the crime itself.
The minister went on to say:
This has produced some arbitrary and rather unsatisfactory results.
The minister has expressed an opinion and I must admit that I am not sufficiently acquainted with the results of the enforcement of this act in Great Britain to advisedly discuss with him this matter of opinion.
Still I am prone to believe that this change on the part of the minister is unadvisable.
Moreover the minister is not in the best position to express such an opinion, and I do not think we have anything to teach the United Kingdom jurists in this matter of legislation on capital punishment.
It is a fact that there has been mass commutations in Britain, 14 death penalties being commuted from April 16 to June 10, 1948.
It should be remembered that, in 1948, a member of the British House of Commons had introduced a bill for the abolition of the death penalty during a 5 year experimental period. This bill was subsequently defeated by a huge majority in the House of Lords.
Here in Canada, in spite of the recommendations from the joint committee and a majority opinion in the house favouring the retention of capital punishment, 39 death penalties were commuted out of a total of 49.
I acknowledge a great respect for British criminal law. In fact, the greatest reforms in this field originated in that country.
Commenting upon the Gowers report, the minister could not conceal that he thought highly of this document when he said, as found at page 5221 of Hansard:
Its report was presented to parliament in the month of September 1953, and it constitutes the most complete analysis of the question in modern times.
It should be noted that all major changes in British criminal law followed intensive

Criminal Code
studies made by jurists and experts in the field, while here in Canada through section 1 of the bill now before us, we reject one of the most important recommendations made by the joint committee.
This new clause dividing murder into two kinds is brought forward as an ordinary government measure.
This new concept of criminal law apparently does not result from any special studies made by jurists or experts in that field.
In that regard, I must say that I hold the highest opinion of the Minister of Justice and all the senior officials of his department. But in all deference and while I recognize the high standards they set for the general administration of the Department of Justice, I do not feel I will reduce their prestige when I say that clause 1, in particular, is not the result of discussions by Criminal Code specialists, by jurists with a considerable experience acquired in criminal courts or by writers of criminal law.
While it is true that the newspapers, following the introduction of this legislation, agreed to that idea of two kinds of murder, several articles have been published since giving us the views of jurists, of experienced men, and I think-the minister has probably seen those articles-that this bill, and particularly clause 1, has been received by several jurists with mixed feelings which raise very important questions.
I have here an article that appeared in the Toronto Star of May 24, 1961, under the heading:
(Text):
Two murder penalties injustice-Ex-Judge
London, Ontario.-Proposed legislation to establish two degrees of murder was described last night by Arthur M. Lebel, retired Ontario appeal court judge, as a system which would make fish out of one man and flesh out of another.
He said if one man hangs and another does not, if one is locked up and another is not, "the sense of justice in all of us will say let us scrap the whole thing... let us not have any capital punishment".
The new government bill on capital punishment separates deliberate murder, punishable by death, and non-premeditated murder, punishable by a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment.
Mr. Lebel told the Canadian Progress club of London that mandatory sentences have never worked and would not work under the proposed new law.
"What will juries do if they do not like life sentences" he asked, and added, "reduce the charge to manslaughter."
Mr. Lebel also criticized the clause which would require cabinet approval for the release of a person sentenced to death but whose sentence is commuted. "What is wrong with the national parole board?" he asked.
He also questioned why there should be any interference from the cabinet when a court and jury find a man guilty of capital murder.

(Translation) :
Mr. Chairman, the minister based the introduction of this bill on the following principle, as reported on page 5223 of Hansard for May 23, 1961:
We have taken account of the fact that the country, as reflected by opinion in this house, favours retention of capital punishment.
Well, there is in law a proverb or a gibe which states:
Law is what it is, and not always what we should like it to be.
Well, what is the purport of clause 1, especially in relation to the other clauses of the bill? I firmly believe that by drawing this distinction between capital and non-capital murder, as set out in clause 1, we lay down premises which will in fact make capital punishment inoperative. More than that, our premises are contrary to the specific distinction made by the minister when he introduced this legislation, convinced as he is in spite of all that, that the country is of the opinion that capital punishment should remain efficient.
It seems to me that in an effort to solve a problem created by the government itself, the government is submitting, through this distinction between capital and non-capital murder, a project whose full implementation is not supported by the statement made by the minister when he introduced the bill. This distinction, provided under section 1, is meant, I think not only to satisfy the government's abolitionists who are getting impatient, even among the most eminent members of the cabinet, but those' who want to keep capital punishment in our statutes. Therefore, we are faced with a compromise that is not realistic and which, in practice, disavows public opinion.
This bill, which is based on the fundamental distinction of section 1 between capital and non-capital murder, has not been sufficiently examined, in my opinion, and section 13, which I may not comment in detail, is evidence of what I claim-this bill, and especially this basic distinction of section 1, has not been studied by experienced law officers and practitioners in criminal law. It is contrary to the recommendation of the joint committee which submitted its report in 1956 and, furthermore, it suggests a legal distinction contrary to the 1957 homicide act of the British parliament.
For all these reasons, I submit there is no urgency to adopt, in its present context, a legal definition based on legal uncertainties

and this distinction between degrees of murder should be reviewed by experienced law officers.
Mr. Chairman, I know that the rules of this house do not allow me, at this stage, to move a motion to this effect, but if I were free to do so I would do so immediately, in order that section 1, as well as the whole bill, be again referred to experts in this field. However, nothing prevents me at this time from renewing my request to the Minister of Justice, and I would remind him of the amount of work accomplished last year by the special committee during the discussion of the Canadian Bill of Rights. In spite of all this work, once we had considered the views of the experts heard in the special committee the subject was again referred to the committee of the whole of this house.
Mr. Chairman, those were the remarks I had to make on section 1. I shall ask the minister, as well as the government, to give serious consideration to that suggestion. I think, that if the minister and the government followed up the idea of reconsidering the bill, it would meet the views of this country's press.
Besides, there is no urgent need to go ahead with this right away; the whole matter might well be reconsidered in a special committee and we could take it up again during this session and pass the bill which the government would then submit. This legislation would be much more efficient. We would thus establish a much less disappointing basis than if we went ahead with the bill in its present form.

Mr. Chairman, unfortunately I was unable to be present during the debate on second reading of the bill, and I should like to avail myself of the opportunity now for a moment or two to put myself on record with regard to this all-important measure.
I thought the debate on second reading was of a character of which all members of the house could be proud. As I say, I should like to put myself on record, and I can best do so by means of a very short quotation from the words used by the Minister of Justice in presenting the bill to the house. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I should like to read a short passage from the minister's words as found on page 5226 of Hansard of May 23:
Finally, we present it in the conviction that in its merciful and progressive provision of an age limit below which no one shall be executed, and of an automatic review by an appeal tribunal to remove so fast as possible the element of human or judicial error, together with its other progressive features, it represents a proper reconciliation between the necessity for the protection of the lives of decent and law-abiding citizens on the one hand, and the desire of a Christian and civilized society to see justice tempered with mercy and forbearance on the other. On this basis we submit it for the approval of the house.
On that basis, Mr. Chairman, I am happy to vote for the bill.

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have not taken part in the discussion of this subject since the matter was first introduced in the house by the hon, member for York-Scarborough in the bill he presented last year. Like other hon. members without exception, I regard the bill as one of the most important projects put before us for consideration and decision. The details of the bill are now before us, and it is possible to examine what the minister has sought to encompass. I think it is important that at this stage we should indicate our feelings as to the extent to which the bill meets the principle involved.

Criminal Code
Murder is the most serious crime in our Criminal Code. Yet this, with our allied offences, is the most difficult of all crimes to define and deal with. Over the week end I spent some time discussing this matter with certain persons, one of whom has had very considerable experience at the bar in criminal matters. In large measure I am influenced by his experience and advice in what I want to say today.
I believe there is more case law on the subject of murder than any other single crime. That statement may not have the significance for those who are not lawyers than it will have for those who are. But if it is a fact that there is more case law on this subject we should be careful about adding needlessly to our jurisprudence in a matter as vital to human beings and to our society as this matter is. It seems to me that because of the extended and far-reaching changes contemplated in this measure we should make sure that we take no final decision without the most thorough study.
I join with the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont in his plea to the minister this morning that at this stage we make sure that we in this parliament give the most careful consideration to this measure. Nothing the hon. member has said or that I am about to say is in any way a reflection on the care which hon. members of this house have given or will give to this bill. However, all of us are members with divided interests and occupations. I take it that none of us are experts in this matter, and that our knowledge of criminal practice, generally speaking, is not such as to give us the authority with which to arrive at a final judgment in this matter when there are at our disposal advice, experience and judicial and professional skills that can assist us greatly, in the light of our common law decisions, to make sure that we are doing the correct thing not only in principle but in the maintenance and furthering of that principle.
I believe, after careful examination of this bill, that one can say that it is not without much ambiguity, and that it is in some respects muddled. No legislature in a matter of this importance would want to pass a bill of this kind if that is the case. I submit that it is the case, and I hope at the proper stage to indicate that fact.
It is a fact-and I am sure the minister will not deny this statement-that many of those who have participated in many murder trials in our country, both for the defence and for the prosecution, are not clear on the meaning of this bill. As I have already indicated, I myself over the week end discussed the matter with a number of individuals who have had a good deal of experience

both as crown prosecutors and as defence counsel, and I may say that is their judgment.
Why this bill has not been sent to a committee of the House of Commons is difficult to understand. I hope the minister, in offering a defence, will not seek to do as he very nearly did the other day, namely suggest that we are inconsistent in the Liberal opposition by making this proposal, in view of the attitude which I personally, on behalf of our party, took in this house the other day when I complained about the contemporaneous sittings of parliamentary committees. This question is too important to be disposed of in that way. If this bill had been introduced early in the session there certainly would have been no real difficulty. I can well understand the minister wanting to see his measures receive ready dispatch, but in a matter of this sort I submit that is not a justifiable position to take.
In the United Kingdom this problem has been confronted and a solution has been put forward which is not the same as the solution provided in this bill. There has been a pinpointing of the instances when punishment by death will be permissible and will be the sanction provided under the law. However, before that decision was arrived at, after much discussion in parliament itself and after much discussion among the people of the United Kingdom generally, a royal commission on capital punishment was appointed.
That commission sat for four years from 1949 to 1953. It is interesting to note that the royal commission had before it the most experienced professional witnesses, including crown prosecutors, defence counsel and, more particularly, members of the judiciary who by their long experience, I think by what they said, proved to be indispensable in the evidence they gave. For instance, there came before the committee Lord Chief Justice Goddard, then the leading criminal judge in Her Majesty's courts.
With all this background they reached a decision. I am not saying it was the right decision, but it was a decision different from the decision which we are providing in a bill the principle of which I have voted for and will vote for. However, I point out that this bill now before us, which is not the English bill, represents a departure from our present law and that fact itself is a matter of the greatest importance.
I hope the minister will not think I am speaking about him personally in what I am about to say, because that certainly is not my intention. I am seeking to be as objective as possible in this matter. I have said that in England a royal commission was appointed and that the royal commission gave to the

lord chief justice of England, many of his colleagues, leading crown prosecutors, leading defence counsel, professors and the like, the opportunity to come and lay before it their opinions as to the formula, legally conceived, which they thought should be provided, to say nothing of the number of people with social welfare interests and others who appeared before the commission. But we have had none of that procedure nor have we had advice from such persons.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: In order that I may be clear with regard to the point my hon. friend is trying to make, may I ask him this question. Do I understand him to suggest that at the time of the Gowers royal commission a bill was then under contemplation? That is not my understanding of the matter.

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: There was no draft bill or proposal before the Gowers commission.

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
That is right. My hon. friend is quite correct. If I gave that impression I did not intend to do so. However, there was discussion of the kind of formula, involving legal precepts, that should be embodied in any kind of bill that would be dealt with. As a matter of fact, in his evidence the lord chief justice spoke of the distinction between various classes of murder and gave an indication of the very phraseology which should be used in order to meet certain particular objectives.
What I am seeking to establish is the fact that the parliament there made a decision only after there had been careful study. We are going to make a similar decision, and we have not had the same study. Who are the authors of this bill? The minister himself is a distinguished member of the bar. I do not in any way wish to suggest anything that would be regarded as the expression of a view that he is not eminently qualified to be Minister of Justice and that he is not a distinguished member of the bar. However, I am not aware that his experience at the bar has been on the criminal side. I am not aware that there is in the Department of Justice at the present time any official who has had great experience in criminal practice. I may be wrong in this, but I gave careful consideration to the point before making the statement. I do not believe there is anyone in the Department of Justice now who has had any experience professionally, either in private practice or as a professional officer of the department, in the field of criminal law. I think this would be very important, if true, in giving us the kind of confidence we would want to have in the absence of
Criminal Code
the study about which the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont spoke a moment ago.
I suggest to the Minister of Justice, as a further argument for no undue haste, that I am sure we could determine this matter within the course of the present calendar year and yet give this measure the kind of study representation and care which I feel must antedate the passage of a bill of this importance. I would be prepared to suggest to the minister that every judge, every defence counsel and every crown attorney would say that in this matter we have not had-I do not say this with regard to the subject matter of the bill, necessarily-the study which this bill deserves. If the United Kingdom took four years to consider this matter, surely we are not asking too much of this parliament when we say it would be worth while to spend more time in the study of this measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, does my hon. friend forget the two years our parliamentary committee spent on the matter?

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
That parliamentary committee was conducted under the chairmanship of my former colleague the hon. member for Essex West. It was a committee that pursued its course with care and responsibility, but the witnesses who were called before it were not all of the character of some of the people about whom I have spoken today. Also, it was a committee that did not deal exclusively with this particular problem; it dealt with a variety of other matters as well.
What objection can there be to having this kind of bill, for instance, submitted to a carefully selected committee of the Canadian Bar Association? That was done, as the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont pointed out, in the case of the bill of rights. The Canadian Bar Association and other interested bodies appeared before a committee and gave their views as to the bill of rights. If the bill of rights was regarded as warranting that kind of treatment, surely a bill dealing with the particular subject matter at hand deserves similar treatment. Yet this bill will not be submitted to these various bodies. The proposal is that we should give it the finality that we give to all measures passed in this house after it has gone through various stages.
I have supported this bill in principle, but even so I believe we would be wise in making sure that we have ourselves given the greatest possible care to this matter, and also that others who by training and experience are particularly competent to assist us have made sure that the drafting, the legal phraseology and the legal formula employed in the bill are such as to enable the proper dispensation

Criminal Code
of justice in the future, both from the point of view of the crown and of those charged with murder.
Some hon. members may suggest, "What is wrong with having the committee of the whole deal with this matter?" I suspect that would be the viewpoint of the hon. member for York-Scarborough. "Why should not every hon. member of this house be given an opportunity of discussing this matter? Why should it be confined to members of the committee?" My answer to that question is that if you have a parliamentary committee, obviously you cannot have the whole house in that committee, but that does not preclude the widest participation by hon. members of this house who are especially interested or especially qualified to deal with this matter; nor does it preclude an ultimate discussion of the committee's deliberations in this house. I am afraid that the bill as drawn up at the present time will provide defence counsel for a long time in the future with all kinds of ammunition which may or may not be in the interests of the administration of justice in our country.
I suggest to the Minister of Justice that the proposal made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont with regard to further study of this matter, enabling those especially qualified to give evidence, is a step which is both prudent and, I believe in the circumstances, urgently necessary if we are to avoid passing a measure of such importance without employing every safeguard that it is possible for us as human beings to resort to in trying to evolve an enactment of the best possible character. I believe that only in this way will we have the feeling that we have taken the right course.
I agree with the basic principle of the bill, which seeks, as I understand it, to provide a distinction between murders for which there is to be the death penalty and other murders. That being the case, it seems to me it is most important that the distinction should be drawn as precisely as possible. If this plea is not accepted, what we will be doing will be passing this bill in as many days as we pass other measures in this house of much less consequence. Are we prepared, as members of parliament, to say that in a matter involving security of the person, life, death and the administration of justice we want to pass a measure without using those instruments of understanding and assessment which were used in the United Kingdom when they were confronted with the same problem a few years ago?
I believe the suggestion made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont is a very worthy one. We should be satisfied that we
[Mr. Martin (Essex East).!
have put into this bill provisions which will allow no room for doubt or uncertainty as to when the death penalty is to be imposed. I do not believe this bill does that.
It would be interesting to know what suggestions could be put forward in that regard. I say this bill is not clear because, as we know, all convictions for murder require the existence of mens rea, or the element of intent. I ask, after reading this bill, what additional elements are required to make a murder a planned and deliberate one. I do not see anything in this bill that answers this question. It is true that this bill makes a distinction, but it is a distinction that is going to offer to defence counsel and any unobjective crown counsel, an opportunity which I do not believe should exist in the interests of justice.
There are some other ideas I should like to express when we come to the appropriate clauses. Even though it is not open to us now to make any amendment along the line suggested by the hon. member who made the proposal for a further study a few months ago, I suggest that the Minister of Justice has a responsibility in this matter. I know he takes that responsibility seriously. I suggest to him that this responsibility can be exercised more carefully at this moment by recognizing the desirability of calling in those who administer the criminal law and asking the views of the law officers of the crown in the provinces- I do not say the attorneys general, for other reasons-and crown prosecutors, eminent defence counsel, the Canadian Bar Association and other interested bodies with strong views for and against capital punishment.
I support the principle of this bill, but I do not have confidence in the measure as drafted, for the reasons I have given.

I did not have the opportunity to take part in the previous debate on this measure at the committee stage, nor when the bill came up for second reading. I listened, however, with great interest to the statement made by the minister on this occasion and have since that time-up until the time of the vote-considered carefully whether I should be in a position morally to vote for it or against it. Fortunately, my colleagues and I in this group as true Liberals were guided by our conscience and our experience in our decision in voting for or against the principle of the bill.
Criminal Code
As far as I am concerned I have always felt in a dilemma, in that I am incapable in deciding whether I am completely for abolition or completely for retention. In spite of the fact that I have had some limited experience as defence counsel in four murder trials, I have not been able to reconcile in my mind that there should be complete abolition, and I have felt there should be retention of the maximum penalty for at least two classes of crime. Therefore I found it within my conscience to vote affirmatively for this bill in principle.
But having regard to the heart of the bill, that is clause 2 of Bill No. C-92, perhaps I may point out that from my own experience and my reading on capital crimes which have occurred within this country it appears that a very high percentage of them-and these figures, so far as I know, are not available -have occurred by reason of the relationship between men and women, whether it be two men fighting, or the husband causing the death of his wife, or the wife causing the death of her husband. I suggest to the minister that because of the intensity of this relationship a deterrent is seldom present regardless of the provisions of the criminal law. When it is considered that, added to this particular fact that crimes arise mainly because of the man-woman relationship, there is the fact that in most Canadian crimes there is an element of the use of alcohol, I think this more than ever points up the fact that a deterrent does not exist; because when one commits such a crime, either arising from the man-woman relationship or because of the excessive use of alcohol, there is no deterrent which works on the mind at that moment.
This being the case, I have felt that if there is any deterrent at all to causing the death of another person it must be the thought of being apprehended, and not of what would occur following that. Perhaps even more so, when one considers a deliberate murder, where one has made a deliberate plan involving more thought, perhaps a higher intelligence, if anything were to deter that person it would be more likely to be life imprisonment rather than the ending of a life by hanging.
Because of the gaps which are in the legislation I would like to identify myself and my remarks, with the two hon. members from my party who have already spoken, the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont and the hon. member for Essex East, inasmuch as I would ask the minister to make arrangements for a further study by those who have had experience in this field prior to bringing the bill to a vote for final decision.

Criminal Code
In particular I would ask the minister why it is that this bill contains no provision for one of the most important things which the public should protect, that is, the possibility of the death of a prison guard during the course of a prison riot. Hon. members will recall that in the last few years there was one of these in the state of Michigan where a Canadian was involved, where there was a riot and a guard was killed. In this incident the Canadian had been sentenced to life imprisonment for murder and could not be sentenced to anything further.
Under the legislation which is now before us, if there is an attempt to escape from prison or lawful custody and a murder is caused, it is a capital murder. However, if there is a riot, during which there is an unpremeditated killing, nothing in this legislation makes this a capital murder. In the interests of protecting those who must work in our maximum security penitentiaries, I suggest the minister should give consideration to this type of killing which, for the general good of the community, should be included as capital murder.
In every case involving a second murder, I suggest it is certainly necessary to retain the death penalty. In the British homicide act of 1957 there is a provision stating that an individual who is convicted of murder for a second time must pay the supreme penalty. While I appreciate that under the provisions of the act before us if a murder is deliberate, whether it be a first or second one, in all likelihood the culprit will pay the maximum penalty, it is not beyond the realm of possibility that an individual could commit two non-capital murders. I suggest that one should not be entitled, to use the phrase of the Prime Minister this morning in respect of another matter, to more than one bite out of the cherry. If an individual is so skilful as to cause the death of two persons on different occasions I submit the state should demand the death penalty in respect of the second murder.
There is another provision contained in the British homicide act of 1957 which I recommend to the minister particularly for the protection of police officers in Canada. I appreciate that English police officers are unarmed, which is not the case generally in Canada. However, in most provinces of Canada police officers are not only ill trained but ill paid, and must assume the risk of dealing daily with criminals and the risk, more than any other private citizen, of thereby being injured or killed, I suggest there are great benefits, for the good of the state and of those people who stand between us and the criminal element, to be derived by the inclusion of that provision of the British

homicide act retaining the death penalty in respect of the killing of police officers.
I can recall, as I am sure all hon. members will, that this has happened once or twice in the last ten years in the province of Ontario, causing great public outcry because of the necessity, in this ever more complex society, of depending upon those individuals to protect us from the criminal element.
Bearing in mind that the present legislation seeks to make a difference between capital and non-capital murder based mainly upon the element of deliberation, whether it be under paragraph (a) or (b), there is no provision in this legislation, as there is in the British homicide act of 1957, in respect of an individual who suffers, not from insanity, as judicially defined, but from diminished responsibility. I should like to refer to section 2 of part 1 of the British homicide act of 1957, which reads as follows:
2. (1) Where a person kills or is a party to the killing of another, he shall not be convicted of murder if he was suffering from such abnormality of mind (whether arising from a condition of arrested or retarded development of mind or any inherent causes or induced by disease or injury) as substantially impaired his mental responsibility for his acts and omissions in doing or being a party to the killing.
Surely this principle should commend itself to the minister and hon. members of this committee. If the essential element to be used in differentiating between non-capital and capital murders is the element of deliberation, these poor unfortunates in our society, many of whom are attracted to a criminal way of life, who are incapable of being completely responsible for their acts who are incapable of that, mens rea which must always be proved, should never be placed in jeopardy of being hanged.
I have in mind, Mr. Chairman, the following situation. A person in full charge of his mental capabilities hires an individual who is mentally retarded to accompany him in committing a bank robbery. The mentally retarded individual equips himself with a weapon. He is not given the weapon by the person who planned the robbery but provides it for himself, so the individual actually in charge of the robbery cannot be convicted of counselling or procuring the other person to acquire this weapon. The two go together to the bank where the one in full possession of his faculties commits the robbery and is the only individual actually involved in the robbery. During the robbery the individual who is mentally retarded, through fright or for some other reason, fires at and kills a person in the bank. As I read the legislation before us the mentally retarded individual, who had not considered murder but who committed murder during the course of the

robbery, is liable to be hanged while the other person, fully aware of what he was doing, not having planned the murder but being unmindful of it, cannot be convicted of a capital offence.
I have outlined some problems and situations which have occurred to me within the last few days. I certainly am not an expert regarding the crime of murder, either as it exists presently or as it appears in this bill. However, I suggest there is in this chamber at the moment an individual who has had experience with a great many cases of this type. That is the chairman of the national parole board, now sitting before the minister. As a magistrate in the county of Welland he frequently presided at preliminary hearings on charges of murder, and I do not know of any individual who has been in a better position to see the day to day effect of such crimes in a community, either from the position of the defence or of the prosecution.
So I suggest to this committee that when someone as inexperienced as I am can make four or five suggestions which require consideration, surely there are many more qualified individuals who should be heard before this committee makes its final decision.
May I call it one o'clock?

Mr. Chairman, on the first full day of discussion of this most important bill I consider it a privilege to take part in the debate. I appreciate the remarks which other hon. members have made, but I must say I find it most unfortunate that, although some members on the government side have spoken for a minute or two, no one has helped hon. members who are to make a decision by an analysis of this most important legislation or have given the necessary details to indicate that this bill meets the requirements of our Canadian society at this time.
Before we vote on clause 1, I trust that members from all sides of the house will have expressed the reasons why they find this is the legislation on capital punishment that is required in Canada today. I trust that we shall not leave it to the Liberal opposition alone to scrutinize this bill which we are now studying clause by clause to ascertain that the protection of our society is fully met by this legislation.
Criminal Code
Although I appreciate the remarks made by the Minister of Justice, I must say that he has in no way given a substantial reason why he supports the new ideas, opinions and laws which he hopes will help to solve this important problem. We know of no public document this government has received which contains instructions or opinions of specialists on the matter. There is no such public document in the possession of any member of the House of Commons. We know of no special committee set up to study this matter and define and phrase a statute of this importance. As I say, we do not know why this bill was not referred to a committee to make sure that it incorporates all the protections which would meet the desires of the Canadian people and possibly the desires of specialists in the matter.
We all recall how the bill of rights was improved by the study given to it by a special committee formed for that purpose. I for one am absolutely surprised at the conduct of this government in asking hon. members to pass upon a bill the phraseology of which we cannot individually analyse, nor do we know the significance of all its details. This is why I should like to see members on the government side of the house give reasons why they feel that clause 1, which we are now discussing, meets in full the desires of the Canadian people.
Recently I said I agreed with the principle of the bill. I am one of those who feel that it is important at this time in our history to solve some of the problems which pertain to capital punishment in our country. This is what we are doing, and this is what the Canadian people whom we represent are thinking about for two or three reasons. I should like hon. members on the government side to realize this and to give opinions which would be constructive in the study which we are now giving to this legislation.
We know there has been difficulty with juries and judges who found their hands tied because the law did not give them the directives required to reach a proper, honest and justifiable decision in the matter. We know also that in Canada people resent the fact that with respect to practically every conviction for murder, where capital punishment is imposed, the final decision rests with the cabinet of this country. I do not wish to discuss the royal prerogative in regard to pardon, but I believe the view is commonly held among people throughout Canada today that we must try to find a way to end the procedure whereby the final court of appeal in murder cases is the cabinet.
We know that in the past the royal prerogatives were limited. I only have to recall to the minds of hon. members the television

Criminal Code
program of a few days ago wherein Baldwin insisted that the crown should not change a law which the representatives of the people had decided to pass. Hon. members know that is so, and I am afraid that the way this legislation is phrased it will bring about a greater degree of inconsistency.

The hon. member for York-Scarborough says no, but I should like to indicate to him the problem that the people of Canada see so far as capital punishment is concerned. Our judges and juries find their hands tied because of the lack of a proper definition of the crime which should deserve capital punishment. On the other hand, I believe the Canadian people do not see any good reason why the final court of appeal with respect to murder should be the cabinet of Canada, which is composed of politicians.
There are three divisions in the administration of the affairs of our country. There is the legislative body, this House of Commons. There is the judicial section composed of judges and juries in accordance with our method of administering justice. We also have the division which is composed of crown attorneys and policemen. Having regard to the problems with respect to capital punishment and the criticisms that are made, I say it is our duty to make sure that, on the one hand, we keep the decision as to capital punishment out of the hands of politicians and, on the other hand, out of the hands of those people employed in the administration of justice.
I find after analysing the bill that it brings about a situation whereby the authority of politicians in the matter of capital punishment is increased, as is the authority of those people who are employed in the administration of justice. It is unfortunate that I can speak on clause 1 only and not go into how it may be related to other clauses of the bill. Members of the house will recall the television program some months ago in which part of the process of hanging was depicted, and which I understand some company refused to sponsor. However, the C.B.C. undertook to make the program available to the Canadian people, and I was impressed by it. If I recall correctly the title of the play was "The Case of the White Horse". If I may give the story briefly, a small community miles from anywhere found that a murder had been committed within the community. Someone had seen a white horse being driven through the town on the night of the murder. No one in the community owned a white horse, and as the town was without any system for the administration of justice they created their own. That is what we are trying to do in this bill and that

is what preceding parliaments have tried to do, create a law whereby people can judge for themselves.

I am not answering because it is obvious to anyone walking the streets who has any brains that parliament is the only body that can make the law with regard to those matters which come within its powers under the British North America Act. Why should an hon. member, especially the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister, ask me whether I feel that parliament should make the law? That is our only function; we have no other. We have nothing to do with the administration of justice or with our judiciary. It was made certain in the British North America Act that we would have nothing to do with the judiciary or with the administration of justice. I am absolutely opposed to the expression of the view by anyone that our jurisdiction goes beyond that of making the law or that we should tell our courts what they should do and what decision should be made. That is why I am speaking on this very subject. That is why I say that in amending the code so far as capital punishment is concerned we should do so in a way that will remove the function of the cabinet in this regard.
I am not saying there is no such thing as the royal prerogative to pardon. That should exist, but it should continue to exist as something to be used only in the most extraordinary circumstances. It should not be embodied in our Criminal Code by making provision, as the bill does, that a jury may ask the cabinet to exercise clemency. I say

that the politicians should stay out of this matter, and our crown attorneys should do likewise. Our crown attorneys should not be able to say that this Canadian citizen will be tried on a murder charge for which the punishment is hanging while another citizen will also be tried for murder but under a charge for which the punishment is not hanging. That is what the bill sets forth.
I heard hon. members speak on second reading of the bill. I heard the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, who said he was opposed to this change if it means that we will be trying to protect the criminal rather than Canadian society. I appreciated what he said, and it is most unfortunate that he is not here today. I should like to ask him to support my views about the bill which gives extended power, in that it practically makes the cabinet a part of our judicial process. It makes the cabinet of Canada the final court of appeal for murder. It also gives crown attorneys and police officers the power to decide who will face hanging if he is found guilty and who will face life imprisonment. I am absolutely opposed to that.

I have a great appreciation for the way justice is administered in Canada, but to give those who administer justice the opportunity, duty and function to decide who is going to face hanging and who is going to face life imprisonment is not in my view the type of improvement in the law that the Canadian people want to see implemented. It is not the type of improvement that the legislators in this house should try to formulate.
I realize that it is most difficult to be precise in describing all crimes and the circumstances that go to constitute each crime. Our duty today is not to get up and congratulate the Minister of Justice on this wonderful bill. Our duty today and this week is to study this bill and see what results it will have in Canadian society. We have no other function but to sit here today, tomorrow and the balance of this week to study this bill, and for that reason I am pleased to take advantage of this occasion during the clause by clause study of the bill to give to the minister some of the opinions I may have. The report was not favourable to a bill of this type. A study of this subject was undertaken in England in 1957, although England has no criminal code such as we have in Canada. Mr. Chairman, I should also like to make a few remarks on the use of the adjective "deliberate", in section 2(a) of the act.
The word "deliberate", according to the dictionaries, does not have quite the same meaning in French as in English. The English word means that someone has done something "without impulse", "without deliberation", while according to the French dictionaries, the word "deliberate" rather means "voluntarily".
I recognize that the Minister of Justice, who considered the English version in the first place, just as I did, will say that if there is any difference as between the English and the French texts in Canada, the meaning of the English terminology must be accepted.
However, I fail to see why a province should always, in regard to that section, have to go by the rule requiring that the English interpretation be the criterion.
I feel we should try to find a translation involving no distinction between the two languages, such as there is now between the words "deliberate" and "delibere".

For instance, on the basis of the French terminology, I would say that a man, finding himself betrayed in his love for his wife, might go into his garage, shed or basement, pick up a gun and kill the guilty party.
There is no doubt that on the basis of the English version, this individual would get away, because his action would have been prompted by an insult. That is what is meant by the word "deliberate".
However, on the basis of the word "deli-bere", he would be guilty, because a man who goes to his shed and picks up a weapon to kill another man does so voluntarily.
Perhaps the distinction is rather fine, but I would remind hon. members that it is important to look at the wording of the bill.

I am just stating the problem.
I realize that if the nurse could prove she had no intent that would be the case, but accused persons are not always in a position to furnish the evidence that is required for a jury to find they had no part in the offence.
I realize that the clauses of this bill do not abolish those matters which may be given in evidence by an accused person, but we are trying to establish when a person shall be judged guilty of capital murder and thereby suffer capital punishment and hang, and when a person shall be found guilty of non-capital murder and therefore will not hang. I am suggesting to the committee that this matter should be given careful consideration. I am not saying that in no way will anybody be able to obtain justice in our courts. I am giving these examples, and more specifically the last example to illustrate my point. I know that if there is absolutely no mens rea and the jury finds there is no mens rea or intent, the person accused cannot be found guilty of murder. I admit that.
However, sometimes these circumstances are not easy to prove. I feel that as we are now considering how the Criminal Code should be worded in order that proper direction shall be given to judges and juries, our consideration should be as complete as possible and the Criminal Code should be worded in a way that would meet to the fullest extent the different circumstances which may arise. I repeat that I am confident no government would be capable of formulating a statute which would satisfy the requirements of the situation 100 per cent. But it is not enough merely to congratulate the Minister of Justice. We have the duty to ensure that whatever measure we do enact will meet the situation to the best of our capacity and knowledge.
I should like to raise one question in particular concerning clause 1. I think the duty of distinguishing in the first instance between the two classes of murder should not rest in the hands of whoever is bringing the prosecution. It will be my intention to suggest later that the whole of clause 7 should disappear. It is my view that everyone committing a capital crime of the nature covered by one or other of the two classes of murder should first of all be charged with the crime of murder to find out whether he is guilty of having committed a murder at all. If a jury found that a murder had been committed by

the accused, then direction would be given to them by the judge to find, further, whether that person is guilty of capital murder or not. In this way all Canadians committing capital crimes would be faced with the same murder charge. It is my view that if this proposal were adopted it would reduce possible confusion among juries. I know how long and difficult are some of the charges made by judges to juries in murder cases.
It is true there are other fields where the crown attorney can make important decisions with regard to the nature of the crime with which an accused person is charged. The most serious example which occurs to me is the case where the prosecuting officer may choose to proceed on a charge of manslaughter rather than murder. But I say that at this time when we are altering the legislation concerning capital punishment, our court officials should no longer be in a position virtually to decide which person is to face a charge involving hanging and which person is to face a charge involving imprisonment for life. I am not prepared at this time to put forward a formal resolution or amendment, but I am sure the discussion on this clause will continue for some time and I shall almost certainly find it necessary to speak further on some of the amendments which are placed before the committee.
There is another feature about this bill which I find surprising. Although the United Kingdom parliament in 1957 exempted from liability to the penalty for capital murder anyone with a certain degree of mental instability, there is a clause here which provides that any man whose birth certificate shows he was younger than 18 when he committed an offence may escape the death penalty, though he may well have the intelligence of a man of 25. But in this country if it is found that a man has the mentality of a 12 year old, which is the Christie case, he can be hung. Surely the penalty for the crime of murder should be attached not to the birth certificate he carries but to his capacity to commit murder, knowing full well what he is doing. Why should a person who has a birth certificate proving that he is younger than 18 escape, although it may be recognized in court that he has a superior intelligence, while a man whose birth certificate shows he was over 18 at the time the offence was committed but whose intelligence turns out to be that of a 12 year old, will incur the fullest rigour of the law? I think the minister should give us an explanation of this point before we proceed very much further.
I appreciate that members of the committee have given me an opportunity to continue

after my time expired. I will avail myself of other opportunities later to discuss certain other phases of the bill.

Editorials and press comments in respect of this legislation have generally been quite favourable. That favourable comment has been more or less based, I suggest, on the assessment that this legislation represents a step in the direction of the abolition of capital punishment. The minister has denied that assessment and, in fact, has quite properly pointed to the fact that this legislation does retain capital punishment. Last Wednesday I voted against this legislation because that vote had to do with

the principle of the bill, the retention of capital punishment. I am personally opposed to capital punishment for two reasons, which I shall attempt to outline briefly.
The first reason is that in spite of all the precautions which may be taken, as well as the safeguards written into the legislation, innocent people have been hanged. We know that as a fact. In my view that fact outweights all the deterrent value of capital punishment, which I understand is the main reason for its retention. The second reason I oppose the retention of capital punishment is that I feel society itself is to some extent responsible for the guilt of accused persons. When an individual is born into this world he is either normal or handicapped. If an individual is born handicapped and later commits murder, there is no way of knowing to what extent the murder resulted from the handicap which he inherited. On the other hand, if an individual is born normal and becomes a criminal, he does so to some extent as a result of his environment. In view of the fact that society is responsible for the environment which leads to the development of that type of individual, it is my belief that society is to some extent responsible for the crimes that person commits.
Since society is responsible for the imposition of capital punishment, that society is to me likened to Pilate washing his hands of the whole business. Furthermore, I believe in the principle that society should not take away something which cannot be restored. When the life of an innocent person is taken away by society in error, that life cannot be restored. I also oppose the retention of capital punishment for that reason.
The curious thing in respect of this legislation is that the minister states it retains capital punishment because of the evaluation of public opinion in Canada as being in favour of retaining the death penalty. I believe it is true that this legislation retains capital punishment on the basis of its deterrent value. I fully agree with that. I think that for the normal person the death penalty is a very strong deterrent, perhaps the strongest there is. But a curious thing about this legislation is that it has abolished the death penalty for all those groups of people who would be most likely to be deterred by it, and it has retained the death penalty for the professional, calculating criminal who is the least likely to be deterred by it. Therefore, on the one hand we are retaining a principle, and on the other we are lessening the deterrent value on which the principle is based.
Surely the object of our legislation should not be to classify types of murder but to

deter killing, to save people's lives and to prevent killing. If a person is killed it does not make much difference whether he is killed by somebody whose crime is going to be classed non-capital or by somebody whose crime is going to be classed as capital murder. It certainly does not alter the fact that the person is dead. What we wish to do is to try to lessen the number of killings. If the deterrent value is valid at all, then we should be extending it, but in this bill we are diminishing it and reserving it only for those groups of people who are least likely to be deterred at all.
As I said, there are some good things in this bill, but I have pointed out one of the objectionable features that my hon. friend inquired about. I think the age limit and the automatic appeal are desirable features, but we are dealing with this legislation in a nonpolitical way. I think the proper thing to do is to send it to a committee where we can get expert opinion from people versed in the practice of criminal law so that we can produce the very best piece of legislation possible. At the same time I think we should inform the people fully as to what the difference is between this legislation and the present legislation, or what we are actually adding to the legislation already in existence because actually when it is evaluated I do not think we are adding very much; in fact, we may be taking away more than we are adding to it.

Therefore, by this legislation I think we shall get a little more proper administration of justice in that we shall have convictions where there should be convictions without fear of too much punishment.

Mr. Chairman, I can make no claim to any legal knowledge or legal education with respect to this matter which would justify my intervention but the matter is such an important one that I feel I should say something about the bill before us, more particularly as I was not able to take part in the debate on second reading.
