... only on rare occasions is this house required to consider and amend or change laws or institutions that form part of the very foundation of our society.
This, Mr. Chairman, is one of those rare occasions. Capital punishment, which is the extinguishing of an individual human life, is certainly not in my view a matter of a politically partisan character when we in this house attempt to deal with it. A bill of this kind, as I see it, deals with fundamental moral values of our society and should be and is being treated in that sense in this house. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, we in the official opposition are not considering this bill in any partisan sense. It has been made clear, so far as we are concerned, that it is a matter for each of us to decide as to how he will vote and the attitude he will take in accordance with his individual conscience and his individual judgment based on considerations of conscience.
The bill has been passed in principle, and if I had been in the house I would have supported its passing. The principle, as I see it, is that capital punishment should not be eliminated but that there should be a limitation on it, through a distinction between murders for which the death penalty is provided and other types of murder. In other

words, there should be a distinction between capital and non-capital murder.
In following the debate and reading Hansard I have been interested to note that there have been those who have opposed the bill for diametrically opposite reasons. In his introduction of the bill the minister stated, and I am paraphrasing what he said, that public opinion in this country was not ready for complete abolition. Perhaps he is right, but I wonder how he has managed to come to that conclusion. Whether or not that is the case, the bill indicates that in the minds of the government this country is presumably ready now to make progress toward the abolition of capital punishment by limiting the categories of murder to which the death penalty is attached.
There are however, some points of very great importance which are related to murder and capital punishment and which are not included within the bill. There is one I should like to mention. I ask myself, why did the government, seeing that it was dealing with this problem, omit reference to the manner or method of execution? In the report of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on capital punishment submitted on June 27, 1956, section 91, page 21, reads in part as follows:
The committee has concluded, after weighing these considerations, that hanging is not the most satisfactory method of execution which might be employed and, accordingly, recommends its abolition.
As hon. members know, that recommendation was made after a great deal of consideration and long and careful examination. The government has not seen fit to accept this recommendation in the legislation before us, and perhaps the minister might be able to give us some information later as to why no action was taken in this regard. It certainly would appear to me, from the study I have been able to give the matter, that there are more humane methods of execution than hanging. As I see it, there could hardly be a less humane method. I cannot understand why the government did not take advantage of this opportunity to deal with that particular problem and perhaps the minister will be able to explain why when he speaks later in this debate.

First, in adopting the basic principle of the bill that there has to be a distinction between murders for which there is to be the death penalty and other murders, surely it is axiomatic that that definition should be drawn as precisely as possible. In a matter of this kind nothing could be much

more important than the maximum amount of precision possible when we are dealing with a question, literally, of life and death. There should be no room for doubt or uncertainty as to when the death penalty is to be imposed and in that sense, as other speakers have pointed out, it seems to me that the bill is defective and that it can be improved.
Murder in general, I admit there can be exceptions to this, requires as an element that there be an intent to kill. We ask ourselves, what additional element or what additional elements, because there may be more than one, are required to make murder planned and deliberate? The bill does contemplate such a distinction, of course, and therefore it would be up to each jury to distinguish between a merely intentional murder and one that is planned and deliberate. It seems to me that we may get into a great deal of trouble in the future in attempting to work out that definition in a way which will not create injustice.
I find it difficult myself to make up my own mind that there is a basic justification for making the imposition of the death penalty turn on that distinction. I know, of course, there can be distinctions in murder and those distinctions have been worked out in legislation in other countries, more particularly in the United Kingdom. However, the distinctions there, as I will try to point out in a moment, are not the same as those embodied in this bill.
Then, there is the effect of this bill, if it should become law, on the deterrent character of punishment. A good deal of consideration has been given to the deterrent effect of capital punishment by speakers who have taken part in this debate. I think it is generally admitted by experts who have given consideration to this matter, Mr. Chairman, and also by the minister himself in his speech, that capital punishment as a conscious deterrent against crime cannot be exactly evaluated. I have, as other members have, read a lot of statistics with regard to this. You can compare the experience of one country where there is no capital punishment with the experience of another country where there is. You can compare the experience of one country during a time when that country had capital punishment, and after it was abolished. You can compare the experience of a state in the United States which has capital punishment with the experience of one that has not. I have not, myself, been able to come to any satisfactory conclusion, merely on the basis of these statistics, because there are too many other factors that may affect those statistics and you are dealing with a question of such fundamental moral
Criminal Code
importance. So I cannot come to any final conclusion, on the basis of those statistics which I have been able to study.
As the minister himself has indicated-I am again paraphrasing his words-it is the effect of punishment in stigmatizing conduct so that the ordinary citizen does not contemplate such conduct that is probably its greatest effect; that is where, as I see it, the deterrent lies. If I may use an expression which has now become a homely one, punishment conditions the mind in the same way as Pavlov's dog was conditioned to salivate when the bell rang. We all have mental blocks created by the existence of punishment against criminal acts. I believe however, that punishment is not, itself a conscious deterrent, except in the case of the professional criminal or in one or two other instances. As the French philosopher Pascal once said, speaking in a different context, "if there were only a small probability of eternal damnation the risk of sinning would appear excessive". Well, that may be true, but it has not prevented sinners from existing in the world for a long time, nor has the existence of capital punishment prevented murder during the centuries that capital punishment has existed. Considering the number of crimes for which capital punishment once was imposed history shows that at times it has not had as much deterrent effect as the reduction in the number of capital crimes has had.
This bill seems to be founded on what I consider to be the shaky basis that a planned and deliberate murder can be deterred by capital punishment. I doubt, in practice, if this will work out. Perhaps I may give one example which was once given a great deal of attention in the press. Not long ago a young man who was crazed by jealousy went out and purchased a knife. He proceeded halfway across the city and stabbed his estranged wife. There is no doubt, Mr. Chairman, that the killing was planned and deliberate. The certainty of capital punishment did not serve as a deterrent. The individual in this case was perhaps beyond the reach, in his mind, of any deterrent. Why should the death penalty apply here, as it would I think if this man, in a momentary loss of control, killed someone yet in technical circumstances which would hardly be interpreted as otherwise than planned and deliberate?
The distinction in this bill between planned and deliberate murder and other murder appears, at least, to give effect to the view- this worries me-that these murders are worse than the others in a moral sense. This interpretation would appear to accept the former

Criminal Code
principle of retribution and vengeance, although I am sure that was not in the mind of the minister when drafting this bill.
Perhaps at this point the minister would permit me to ask him a specific question with which he might be willing to deal now. I think it is a question that has already been asked this afternoon by the hon. member for Niagara Falls while I was out of the house. If during the course of a riot in a prison a guard were killed by the prisoners, would the charge of capital murder be laid against the prisoner committing the offence? As I understand this bill, if the guard were killed under those circumstances, the murder might well not be planned and deliberate and therefore might not be subject to the death penalty. If that is a correct interpretation, does the minister not feel that this would place the prison warden and the prison guards in an intolerably dangerous situation? Would it not discriminate against them, in that sense?
The homicide act of the United Kingdom, as has been pointed out by other speakers, rests on a very different basis from that of this particular bill. The British act, by selecting certain types of killings or certain types of victims, is aimed at the professional criminal, and at the protection of policemen or prison wardens who come in contact with professional criminals; also to prisoners under life sentence who otherwise would have nothing to lose by committing another capital crime. The obvious purpose of the United Kingdom bill is to create a deterrent, and as I mentioned earlier, where a deterrent would be most likely to be effective.
In his statement the Minister of Justice suggested that there were certain murders that would be covered by this bill which would not be dealt with by the British legislation, and that of course is quite true. On the other hand, I suggest there will be murders covered by this bill for which there is no justification in applying the death penalty in one case and not in the other. In other words, I suggest there is greater uncertainty in the division of crimes in this bill than in the British measure. I know that in Great Britain at the present time there is a good deal of uneasiness because there is that uncertainty over their act and how it is working out.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the course recommended by more than one speaker in this discussion is one that should be followed. This bill would stand over so it could be submitted to a committee, where representations from experienced law enforcement agencies could be heard, where evidence could be taken bearing on the actual clauses of the bill, where organizations like

the Canadian Bar Association could offer their views on the details of this bill and where provincial deputy attorneys general could be given the same opportunity. It seems to me it would be wise if this bill were submitted to a committee so that this course of action could be followed. If that were done, we in this house would have the advantage of the experience, judgment, evidence and views of those people, some of whom I ventured to mention a few moments ago.
I should also like to suggest-and I do it in a constructive way-that with a bill of this kind, with a matter of such fundamental moral character, with a matter dealing with life and death, when we are entering into new ground in this country, where the results may be very good but where, on the other hand they may not work out as we hope, it would be wise to include something in this bill which would provide for its reexamination and possible revision at the end of a certain period of years. I hope the minister will give consideration to this suggestion.
It is quite clear that organized society has been progressing now for generations in its attitude toward the death penalty. I think- and I am quite frank in saying this-this bill is a step further in that progress; yet there is certainly no reason to assume that this bill, and I am sure the minister does not make that assumption, has achieved any finality in dealing with such a complex problem.
That being the case, I have put forward two proposals. One is that this bill be given further consideration before a committee, and second, that some provision should be put in the bill to make sure its term of application is limited so it can be re-examined at the end of that time. As I have said, I feel that in some of its details this bill is defective. It is our desire on this side of the chamber, those of us who support this bill in principle, to make it more effective. In due course, when we get to the detailed consideration of the clauses, we will put forward some changes which we hope will have that result.

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I know it is often said by speakers in this house that they had no intention of participating in the debate. I can assure you, sir, that on this occasion that statement is not a mere formality.
I took the attitude that in view of the tremendous amount of study that had been given to this question by the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General there was no reason why I should say anything regarding a matter in which over the years I have had more than a passing interest.

All of us in the practice of law have had from time to time the opportunity of appearing either for the crown or the defence. I belong to that group in the practice of law composed of those who have never appeared for the prosecution in a murder case. I have often said that I had an outstanding record as a crown prosecutor, for I never lost a case. However, that statement is somewhat diminished in importance when I add that from the time of my appointment until I resigned after a change in the government in Saskatchewan I had no prosecutions. However, I have been intensely interested in this problem of capital punishment and have expressed myself strongly on this subject on many occasions, the major reason for that being the possible conviction of an innocent man.
I am not going to go into the problem of the retention of capital punishment as against its abolition. The Leader of the Opposition says statistics can establish anything that the person producing them desires in that field. It will never be possible to look into man's mind and determine an answer to this question which has exercised the thinking of men in every generation, but it is of interest-and this is a fact-that in upper Canada during the first 25 or 30 years of the nineteenth century capital punishment was imposed for a variety of offences.
I remember my old grandfather telling me that he was present at an execution in upper Canada when he was a boy. It was the execution of one charged with pickpocketing. The execution was at Aurora, I think, or one of those localities immediately north of muddy York, as it then was. Everybody gathered from the surrounding countryside, and a number of Scots residents of that area had their pockets picked while witnessing the execution of one for the same offence.
Only recently I read the record of that era by one who has made a great study of punishment and I find there was justification for that penalty. However, one of my major concerns has been the danger of the execution of someone who had not committed the offence. I can do no more than say that this fear is not unjustified by actual experience in our country.
I do not think it is general, but when one innocent man is executed it shows the irrevocability of capital punishment. In order to meet that situation, a great deal of study has been given to the matter of ensuring that anyone accused of murder shall have available to him all of those defences and safeguards that would be available to anyone else.
I think in this legislation we are meeting the danger that is inherent in trials. The human factor is always present. However, we
Criminal Code
have endeavoured to meet it by certain safeguards. I am not going into the particulars, but I think the major safeguard is the automatic appeal. There are others to which reference could be made.
Nothing has caused me, as Prime Minister, more concern than the coming before cabinet of the various cases, after conviction of murdering, when the question arises as to the exercise of the royal prerogative. It is a frightening experience. Over the years in Canada the responsibility in this has rested upon the governor general in council.
I know hon. gentlemen opposite who have served in the cabinets of this country realize something of the experience it is to examine with care and attention the evidence and also the reports which are given by the officials and the recommendation by the judge. It is a responsibility which I feel should be taken from the shoulders of the entire cabinet. In the United Kingdom the home secretary exercises the royal prerogative. He recommends the course to be followed. I am informed that he does not consult other members of the cabinet though he does communicate in difficult cases, as he sees them, with the prime minister for consideration. We have built up over the years-and I am not criticizing it-a routine whereby the cabinet considers these matters, and anyone who has gone through the experience knows something of the awful weight of responsibility that is felt by those who have the duty to examine death sentences and recommend whether or not those sentences should be carried out.
I feel this legislation will go a long way to ensure that mistakes shall not take place. At the same time it will provide juries with an opportunity-one which they have so seldom realized in the past that they have possessed-to recommend mercy when an individual has been found guilty of capital murder. On many occasions I have encountered cases where members of the jury have said after a trial, "If only I had known I could have recommended mercy I would have done so". As far as recommendations of mercy are concerned, there has been no inconsistency on the part of the cabinet in accepting such recommendations. They have always been followed by this government. In the period from 1930 to 1957 there were some 30 recommendations to mercy to which effect was not given by the cabinet. I feel that responsibility for carrying out the law and maintaining the safety of the public in each area depends on the jury. Having heard the evidence and having come to the conclusion on the basis of the law as explained to them by the judge that a verdict of guilty is the only one they can bring in, a jury ought none the less to

Criminal Code
have the right to add a recommendation to mercy, and having done that, to hope that the royal prerogative will be reasonably carried out. I am not dealing with the future now; I am dealing with the period during which I have been in office as Prime Minister. In that period we have concluded that where recommendations to mercy are made, the proper weight should be given to them. How to meet the circumstances and take from the cabinet this responsibility is something to which I have always devoted my thinking. I feel we might well adopt a course analogous to that adopted in the United Kingdom today whereby the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General would make the determination and recommendation and, on the basis of the opportunity now given to juries to recommend mercy, would be able to bring their recommendation to the cabinet as a whole. That recommendation, excepting in extraordinary circumstances ought to be accepted.

No. The hon. gentleman was speaking to his seatmate at the moment I was discussing that. What I said was that I feel this is the practice which might be followed. I do not expect it to be followed, but it may be considered, for many hours taken by the cabinet in consideration of these cases-and it takes hours if they are to be examined honestly and conscientiously-might well be saved, now that juries are going to be asked directly whether or not they recommend mercy. Responsibility now rests squarely upon the jury to determine in its area and on the particular facts of each case what is just and fair, what constitutes the proper course to be followed in the opinion of those who have heard all the evidence and live in the community in which they are desirous of maintaining justice and equity as between the crown and the subject.
Before the hon. gentleman asked me that question I was about to say something about the degree of recidivism among those tried for murder or convicted of murder. It is a strange thing; in almost every other type of offence the proportion of those convicted who return to the penitentiary is very high. I am not certain what the percentage is, but I think it runs up to 65 per cent and possibly even higher than that. But in the cases of those who have been tried for murder, of

those who have been convicted of murder and subsequently reprieved, and of those who have been tried for murder and convicted of manslaughter, it is of interest that over the years there are very, very few cases where the offence of homicide has been repeated. Indeed, I know of only one such case in this country in my time, a case which took place in the city of Saskatoon. This man was tried for murder and the jury acquitted him of murder but convicted him of manslaughter. He served his prison term and then, in about 1945, he went over to the United Kingdom where he committed murder and was executed.
There is another case which comes to my recollection, and this was in the province of Manitoba. A man was convicted of murder, reprieved and set free. Subsequently he committed a further murder. In one case a second murder was committed in Canada and in the other a man convicted of manslaughter in Canada was executed for the crime of murder in the United Kingdom. But it is amazing to note the number of men who, having served their term in the penitentiary after being convicted of murder, have made good. If I were ever to begin discussing this I could go on indefinitely but I do think of one case, the case of a young man who was charged and found guilty of murder. He killed his father in circumstances which did not result in a recommendation to mercy. He was reprieved, and served 12 or 13 years in penitentiary. I recall so well in 1941, or 1942 speaking to the then minister of justice, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, informing him of this man who, having been educated to the extent of passing into grade 2, spent years in penitentiary as a model prisoner. While in penitentiary he took the remainder of his elementary education and finally passed grade 12 examinations. He had been an exceptionally exemplary prisoner and was in charge of the commissariat of the penitentiary. Upon his release he joined the army and became a sergeant. That man has not changed his name today, and occupies a high position relative to his ability and capacity in the business world in this country.
I can think of another individual who today, and during the years, has done a great deal to elevate a woman who, by reason of circumstances, had fallen away from the path of rectitude. That woman was charged with killing her child.
I could mention immediately six or seven other equally dramatic cases involving individuals who, having been punished, have been able to take their places in life.

I think this legislation will, in the days ahead, be looked back upon as a great forward step. Every avenue has been canvassed with a view to assuring that we shall protect law abiding citizens from what the Leader of the Opposition referred to a moment ago as, deliberate acts of those who desire to live above the law. We shall at the same time leave to juries the right which belongs to them, but which they have not had, to recommend mercy as of right. Up to the present time no judge has had the right to ask the jury whether or not it will recommend mercy. In many cases the jury would have recommended mercy if it had the right. From now on the responsibility will rest on the individual conscience of the community to preserve justice.
The Leader of the Opposition suggested that we should postpone this legislation until another session, or at least postpone it until further examination could be made. This is a matter which has received the attention of the Minister of Justice for a considerable period of time. His law officers and all those connected with the administration of justice have studied this measure. It is designed to ensure that we shall protect and preserve our people against those who would place themselves above the law while, at the same time, protecting those who, in passion or under circumstances short of deliberation, commit homicide. It has been said that most of us would, under circumstances of sufficient provocation, do that which we abhor. This legislation is designed to preserve and maintain the abiding principles that must characterize the administration of justice, while at the same time tempering justice with mercy. I cannot agree that we should postpone the consideration of this measure.

Moreover, Mr. Chairman, I was only following the example set by the Prime Minister, who did give rather extended explanations on this recommendation to the jury. The Prime Minister is entitled to his opinion, I have no objection to that, but I think the actual section is dangerous which requires the judge to ask publicly whether the jury is prepared to recommend mercy or to refuse it.
Under the present system, following his summing up of the proceedings, the judge says to the jury: "On the basis of the evidence which has been submitted, you may recommend mercy, but it is not an obligation.
If we included in the act a section under which the judge, following his summing up of the proceedings, would have to indicate to the jury that they are entitled to recommend or not to recommend mercy, but would let them retire to the jury room and reach their decision in complete freedom from pressure, fear or false sympathy for the accused, and outside the presence of the public, the accused, the judge, the friends and the whole family of the accused-whose members would all be in tears-I think it would make things much easier and would be much more in keeping with the role of a jury.
On the other hand, I think the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) was completely justified in suggesting a moment ago that the bill be referred to a special committee of the house, similar to the one we had in 1956.
I also note that only one of the many recommendations contained in the report of the special committee has been followed. I refer to the exemption from the death penalty for persons 18 or under.
All the other recommendations have been ignored, particularly that one.
Here is what we find, for instance, in section 69 of the report:
In practice, the committee feels that any new definition of the crime of murder should closely conform to the present practice of commuting death sentences.
Nor should commutations of death sentences become the general rule. They should remain exceptions as they were in the past.

In the last three years, out of 49 sentences, 39 were commuted. In other words, commutation has become the general rule. I think that is a dangerous practice and that the bill is also dangerous because it is not clear.
To take the example cited by the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis), suppose two armed men enter a bank, and one of them fires a shot. The one just stands there, because he has not been told to shoot. Of course, section 1 of the bill does say:
-or assisted in causing.
And the former section 202 stated:
__facilitating the commission of the offence-
However, there is one point that smart lawyers usually bring up before the jury; they say: do not forget the intent of the lawmakers.
I can see the contradiction that any smart lawyer will point out to the jury. He will say: The intent of the lawmakers was this: However, only the person who actually committed the act or applied the force causing death, or counselled the doing of it, would be guilty of capital murder.
All other murder Is made non-capital.
On that basis, smart lawyers will finally manage to secure the release of many criminals until such time as they personally commit other crimes, or until such time as five or six cashiers have been killed and five or six murderers have been arrested. Furthermore, it is stated in subsection 1:
(1)	Murder is capital murder or non-capital murder.
(2)	Murder is capital murder, in respect of any person, where
(a) it is planned and deliberate on the-
Well, what about the incendiary who puts a house on fire, thus causing the death of one or two persons? He may plead that he had no intention to kill, but just to burn down the house. How do you expect to condemn him when this bill is passed? I think that he enjoys much too great a protection in this case.
Moreover, how would the law deal with cases of rape particularly, when a man, a sadist, gets hold of a three or four year old child, and after committing his crime mutilates her so that she dies? He may say that he had no intention to kill the child, but merely to have his way with her.
Therefore, I repeat that not only should we not attempt to reduce the number of cases which may entail capital punishment, we should rather increase it, more particularly with regard to cases of rape committed on young children and other such cases, also in respect of the drug traffic.

I also think-and in this respect I take issue with what the leader of my party said a few moments ago-that we should not think of modifying the method of execution.
We have capital punishment by hanging, and all honest people seem to be horrified at the idea. Well, it is precisely what I wish preserved: that fear, that shame, that revulsion at the idea of a hanging.
I think that if it has such a critical effect on people who want to retain capital punishment-as they maintain that this method of execution is inhuman-the means must be the right one for deterring those who, though inclined to kill, would nevertheless be afraid of risking such an ignominious fate.
For all those reasons, and many others, which I will have an opportunity to deal with later, when we examine the bill in detail, I think that, except if much stronger arguments than those that have been submitted today are brought forward, I shall be once again obliged to oppose the passing of this bill when we are asked to cast our votes.

Mr. Chairman, while some of the words of the Prime Minister are fresh in my mind I should like just briefly to intervene once again. I am sure the committee listened with considerable interest to what the Prime Minister had to say, particularly in the light of the fact that he has had some considerable experience at the criminal bar. However, I do not feel-and I say this with great respect-that his remarks today, interesting as they were, really answered the queries put on this clause by those of us who have spoken thus far. I may say I do not believe that he fully addressed himself to the clause, but I am not making that observation by way of complaint except to say that, interesting as his remarks were,
I do not feel they answered some of our concerns.
The Prime Minister said he was greatly concerned, and not without reason, that we take steps to avoid the possibility of providing in the future for undeserved convictions. Indeed, he noted there have been persons hanged who were not guilty of the crime for which they were convicted. I suppose no one will deny that. We do know positively that that has happened in the United Kingdom and I suppose it is true elsewhere. I am not aware at the moment of a case in Canada where we definitely know that to be so but it may be true here as well.
But it should be noted that the bill does not avoid that danger. It will still be possible under the bill for an innocent person
90205-6-3494
Criminal Code
to be convicted and, having been found guilty of capital murder, to receive the death penalty. Therefore the bill does not remove that danger. Admittedly it minimizes the occasion. It does provide certain safeguards and I strongly approve some of the safeguards provided in the bill, but the fact is that the bill does not remove altogether or to any appreciable extent the danger of someone being convicted and hanged for a crime for which he or she may not be responsible.
The Prime Minister spoke of the exercise by the crown through the cabinet of the royal prerogative of commutation. I had misunderstood his remarks. At one point I thought he said that the cabinet should be relieved of this responsibility entirely but I gather that is not what the Prime Minister suggested because he went on to point out later that consideration might be given to assigning to the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General the responsibility for dealing with recommendations for mercy.
The Prime Minister observed that in the United Kingdom the home secretary exercises this responsibility without reference to his cabinet colleagues, and undoubtedly the precedent in the United Kingdom served to suggest to the Prime Minister that this responsibility in Canada might be left with the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General. The Prime Minister was talking about a very interesting proposal, but it is to be noted that the bill about which the Prime Minister was speaking does not provide for the delineation of the royal prerogative in that way.
There would be nothing to prevent the Minister of Justice introducing a bill to restrict and define the powers of the cabinet with regard to commutation. As a matter of fact, the royal prerogative in most particulars is now part of the statute law in one way or another. The royal prerogative exercised in regard to commutation with respect to cases of individuals charged with murder is, of course, not a part of the statute law but there would be nothing to prevent a provision in this or in any companion measure to lay down the limit or the extent or in whom in the cabinet should repose the responsibility to give consideration to recommendations of mercy. Therefore all that the Prime Minister's suggestion in this particular amounts to is that it was sort of obiter dictum on his part, one that might represent the practice in the future without giving it any foundation or authority in law.
I would think, however, that it would be wrong for the cabinet in the future, notwithstanding its preoccupations, to assign to the Minister of Justice and to the Solicitor General in the absence of some statutory

Criminal Code
direction the responsibility that now is borne by the cabinet as a whole. If the practice is to be developed of leaving this matter to a committee of the cabinet or to two members of the cabinet, the legal advisers, then I think some authority should be provided in some statute passed by the house for the assignment that is given and for the restriction that is placed on the exercise of the prerogative.
The whole matter of the exercise of the royal prerogative in this regard has, of course, become a matter of great interest since this government came into office because, as the Minister of Justice has noted on other occasions, the number of commutations since 1957 has been very great. I am not quarrelling with any decisions of the cabinet in that particular. I am sure that in the consideration of capital cases the members of the present cabinet applied themselves conscientiously and seriously in accordance with their judgment and their conscience. I am equally sure that this has been the standard of conduct of former cabinets. Certainly it was true of the cabinet of which I had the honour to be a member. I am sure it has been the practice of all cabinets in Canada regardless of political complexion to give this matter the most thorough and objective assessment. But I think it is true to say that just as the conscience of the lord chancellor has varied with the person of the particular lord chancellor so too have the standards resorted to by cabinets at various times in Canadian history in the exercise of the royal prerogative varied considerably.
I know, and I am sure the Minister of Justice will confirm this, that one distinguished minister of justice before the first world war was so concerned about the jurisprudence, as it were, which he thought should serve as a background for cabinet action in capital cases that he laid down a set of principles which he considered should be borne in mind by Canadian cabinets in the consideration of the exercise of clemency. I do not believe that the principles as conceived by that distinguished minister of justice was followed very long even by the cabinet of which he was a member, nor to the best of my knowledge has it been followed by succeeding cabinets. Each human being in the cabinet has sought to exercise his best judgment in accordance with conscience, in accordance with standards of what was thought to be just, what was extenuating, what was relevant in the circumstances.
It seems to me that so far as one can detect in principle this bill does represent the basic standards that have been laid down by the present government in the exercise of the royal prerogative with regard to capital

cases. I have no right to say that this is so.
I have no right nor am I attempting to ascertain what goes on in the cabinet, but I suspect that since the Minister of Justice has brought forward this bill it represents fairly generally the standards which the cabinet itself has applied in considering the various requests presented to it for clemency or commutation. In other words, since the government came into office only those have been hanged who have been guilty of capital murder. I am not quarrelling with that because each cabinet has the right to decide the standards which it feels should be employed in the exercise of the prerogative. If that is the case, I do not see any reason why the government should not say so frankly. I do not see why the government should not put in this bill, or in a companion measure, what it feels are the correct standards for delineating the extent of the exercise of the royal prerogative, a prerogative which has been defined in most instances and has been restricted in many instances. There could not be any reason why there should not be a clear definition in this particular instance.

In the event of a refusal, in the face of such an invitation, this will serve to give some indication to the cabinet of the jury's estimate of the situation, although the Prime Minister did not add those words. The Prime Minister, I think, misunderstood the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition, a suggestion that had been made earlier by the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont and supported by other members of this party who spoke earlier this morning. No one was suggesting that this matter be postponed. I regret that the Prime Minister has preoccupations outside that prevent his listening to this particular portion of my remarks. What we did recommend was that, because of the importance of this matter, we should not pass this measure hastily. We should resort to the various procedures that are open to us to make sure that our final judgment is attended by the most thorough consideration.
We have pointed out that it would be desirable in a matter of this sort, where there is alleged ambiguity, to refer the matter to a committee. One former judge who has had considerable experience in criminal work in the supreme court of the province of Ontario, Mr. Justice Lebel, in a speech delivered last week in London, criticized the bill because of ambiguity. I am sure from my personal knowledge, as I said this morning, and from consultations with certain individuals who have acted as crown prosecutors and defence counsel, that they share the view there are many ambiguities and many uncertainties in the wording of this bill. The consequences of this will be to afford the best counsel a field day and for a long time to come there is going to have to be built up new jurisprudence to take care of the new phraseology in this bill.
For example, there are the words "planned and premeditated". Does planned mean premeditated? This is not defined in the bill. What the Minister of Justice says in this debate will not give substance to the matter because the court, in the interpretation of our statutes, does not look at these debates. Not only does the court not look at them but it is no allowed to do so. Then, we can ask ourselves, what does deliberate mean? I ask, does deliberate mean that the offender is in full control of his reason? Now, that is a very important element in this matter. Does deliberate mean that the offender was in full control
Criminal Code
of his reason? Unless there is a satisfactory answer to that, I am sure it will be very difficult to get a satisfactory solution. These are questions which are not answered in this bill, and the answers to which might be provided if there were a careful study made by a committee before which competent witnesses could be called to assist us in arriving at the most precise language possible.
I do regret that the Prime Minister is not here because I am sure he would have been impressed with the purpose behind this suggestion. This is not a political measure. This is a measure toward which every member is directing his most honest efforts. We have invited the use of parliamentary committees, just as we have in connection with less important measures, for the purpose of preparing the most careful legislative enactment on a matter of this importance. We should ask the best qualified people in our country for their recommendations, in the light of their experience based upon their professional skill. We are not going to have an opportunity of doing that unless the minister accepts our request.
I should have liked to suggest that not only crown prosecutors, defence counsel with criminal law experience, but also judges should be called before this parliamentary committee. I should have liked to suggest that some of the best judges we have in this country, some of those whose work has been in the criminal courts and who because of that have a special ability and a special opportunity to make a most constructive contribution, should be called before the committee just as was done in England. As I pointed out this morning, the learned Chief Justice Lord Goddard, than whom at that time there was no more distinguished criminal law judge, was called to give evidence. The minister knows better than I, I believe, that his recommendations were incorporated to a large extent in the homicide act passed in Great Britain a few years ago. We are not asking that this bill be postponed. This bill can become law this year. We are asking that in addition to our own deliberations we have the support of the Canadian Bar Association, judges, crown law officers at the federal as well as provincial level and other bodies who will give us their judgment, in the light of their competence and experience, with regard to a measure that is so vital, I repeat again, to the security of the individual and to human life in our country.
The Prime Minister himself gave some encouragement that our plea may yet be heard, because when we urged upon him that the bill of rights should be preceded by consideration in a parliamentary committee for

Criminal Code
the purpose of calling the bar association and others before that body the Prime Minister at first said he did not propose to have the bill considered by a committee. However, it is on record that as a result of further urging the Prime Minister took another look at this matter and decided it was in the interests of the bill that it should be sent to a committee for consideration.
That bill was considerably modified. It was made a better document, as everyone knows from the admission of the Prime Minister himself. If that was justified, as I believe it was in the case of the bill of rights, surely it is justified in this case because this is such an important matter. It is a matter that has such vital application to our administration of justice, an administration of justice which characterizes our form of society and of which we are justifiably so proud.
That being the case, I would think that in a matter of this sort the government would want to think twice before passing this bill through with these uncertainties and these gaps, in the absence of steps being taken to provide the best available commentary from the outside. I can only renew that plea.
When the Prime Minister spoke today I hoped that in the light of his experience he would talk about something else that is left out of this bill. I refer to the mode of punishment. In the debate we have had on this bill, and in the discussions which took place on the bill introduced by the hon. member for York-Scarborough last year, not only have we discussed whether or not it was right to punish murder by death but we have also discussed whether or not, in the event that capital punishment was maintained in some form, the mode of punishment should be by way of hanging.
Some strong views were expressed in that regard in this house and throughout the country. I for one believe that the present mode of punishment of hanging an individual is not the method we should continue to use in this country. I believe we should resort to some other more humane, more civilized method of punishment. This is a gap in the bill that was not referred to by the Prime Minister. I should have thought that with his considerable experience at the criminal bar this would have been one matter to which he would have directed his attention.
I ask the Minister of Justice to indicate at some point in our proceedings before too long whether or not he feels that even at this hour the cause of justice and the legislating of the most effective enactment will be served by seeing that this bill does not pass merely on the discussion in committee of the whole.
It is not a question of our ability; it is not a question of our sincerity. We are all anxious

to do the best that can be done in this regard. However, I do feel that where we are making such a fundamental departure in the law with regard to the punishment for murder we should be able to say we have taken every step possible to determine the validity and wisdom of the course which is before us.
I for one do not feel we could answer that question in the affirmative unless the request that this matter be considered by a committee of this house, with all the advantages that affords, is granted by the government and supported by the membership of this house.

Mr. Chairman, I think it would perhaps be useful if at this stage I made some comments by way of reply to what has been said in debate today. I recognize that we are here discussing, in our consideration of clause 1 of this bill, what really amounts to the principle of the bill; that is, the question of whether or not murder should be divided into two categories, capital and non-capital.
For this reason I have raised no objection when on occasion I have felt, as I am sure you have also, sir, that the discussion has ranged pretty widely afield and that, indeed, rather than having a general discussion related to clause 1 we were quite frequently redebating the principle of the bill, which of course was decided when the vote on second reading took place.
However, as I say, since I suppose it might be said that the clause now before us, which will have the effect of dividing murder into capital and non-capital categories, is indeed the main substance of the bill, not too great objection should be taken. However, because of the wide ranging nature of the debate it seemed to me that the most appropriate course for me to follow at this stage would be to make some general observations in reply; to comment, as it were, on the matters raised by outlining our approach and the reasoning and logic which has led us to arrive at this principle of the division of murder into capital and non-capital categories. In doing so, of course, I will answer in a general, if not a particular way, much of what has been said by hon. members who have spoken today. Then, after that, I will go on to deal with some of the specific comments and suggestions that have been made.
In giving this general outline let me do so point by point. First I would emphasize this point. This is important, particularly in light of what in my submission, with the greatest good will in the world, I cannot regard as other than a complete misapprehension in principle on the part of the hon. member for Essex East. I refer to the hon. member's

apprehension that this bill changes the jurisprudence with regard to murder.
Let me first make it abundantly clear that this bill does not change the jurisprudence or the law with regard to murder. We have been deliberately careful not to do that and we have been, as an examination of the bill will show, successful in that objective, namely to leave the existing definition of murder, and therefore the jurisprudence built up with regard to that definition, entirely unchanged.
Second, I should like to emphasize that what the bill does by virtue of clause 1 and the succeeding clauses, is to raise a new question; not a question related to the definition of murder, but a new question which arises only when and if in a prosecution murder is proven. This question that arises is one of fact for the jury.
Therefore there is no new jurisprudence and there is no change in the jurisprudence being created by this bill. The jury will still have to be satisfied that murder has or has not been proven, and in charging the jury on that point judges will rely upon the existing jurisprudence. The question which then arises as a result of the bill is: is the murder which has been proven capital murder or non-capital?
This is my third point in this connection. We have made this question, as a matter of deliberate approach, a question of fact for the jury. It is as a matter of deliberate approach that we have kept the question as simple as possible. It has been urged upon us that the bill lacks something because it does not go into great detail by way of attempting to define, as in a legal treatise, what it is that the words used should mean in law.
We have deliberately avoided that approach and have kept the question as simple as possible. We have kept it a question of simple fact for determination by the jury, and the question is this: was the killing, which the jury has found to be murder, planned and deliberate, or was it not? That is all the jury has to ask itself: was the killing planned and deliberate, or was it not? In my submission, Canadian juries are not incapable of answering that question. Of course, they will be assisted by judges in the interpretation of those words. Jurisprudence will undoubtedly be built up over the years as to what those words mean, and the interpretation given to them will form precedents for other cases. That is how our law develops. But surely this parliament is not going to shrink from establishing a foundation for new law in this field which parliament and our country have desired to be brought into closer harmony with present day concepts of crime
Criminal Code
and punishment. Surely it does not constitute criticism but, properly accepted, praise of this bill to say that it does lay the foundation for the development of a new approach.
My submission is that we have laid such a foundation on the basis of the most simple principle possible, that is, by leaving it to the jury on the basis of whether or not a murder is a planned and deliberate killing. If the answer to that question is in the affirmative, then the murder is a capital murder. If it is not, if the answer is in the negative, then murder is a non-capital murder and is punishable by imprisonment for life.
Some hon. members have raised the question-indeed they have gone further and made the suggestion-that the effect of this legislation will be that there will be no more capital punishment. Such an assumption is totally unwarranted by anything which occurs in the bill, nor can it be deduced from any of the arguments which have been advanced in support of the legislation. The bill preserves the death penalty but provides that it can only be applied in cases where a jury finds an element of deliberation, either in accordance with the words "planned and deliberate" or through the application of section 202. The death penalty is preserved and is applicable in cases where the jury answers those questions in the affirmative.
To suggest that there will be no more cases where captial punishment is imposed is to assume one of two things, neither of which in my submission can really be expected. The first is that there will never again be a planned and deliberate killing in Canada. I wish one could assume that that could be the case, but I doubt whether anyone in this committee would make that assumption. Alternatively such an argument infers that juries confronted with the clearest evidence of a planned and deliberate killing will refuse to find such a verdict. I have too much confidence in the juries of this country to believe that when evidence is presented which satisfies them that the murder has been planned or deliberate or covered by section 202, they will be so perverse as not to bring in a verdict accordingly. I do not accept such a suggestion, particularly in the light of the fact that a great forward step has been made in this bill, namely, the division of murder into capital murder and non-capital murder as a result of which juries may find a man guilty of murder of a non-capital kind in the sure knowledge that he will not automatically be sentenced to hang as a result. This, as everybody knows, has been the great difficulty encountered by juries in the past and it is one of the reasons why juries have been so reluctant on occasion to bring in verdicts of guilty even when the murder charge has

Criminal Code
been supported by the clearest evidence, and why they have so often preferred to find the accused person guilty of manslaughter.
Now juries will be placed in what, in my view, is the proper position. Where the charge is one of capital murder they will decide whether or not the murder has attached to it the element of planning and deliberation which parliament has said to be necessary in order to constitute capital murder. Then, if the jury decides that there was that element of planning and deliberation, I do not believe any hon. member opposite would go so far as to assert that in these circumstances they would not bring in a verdict of capital murder. That is, in effect, what hon. members opposite have said when they have suggested that after this bill becomes law there will be no cases where capital punishment is imposed in Canada.
The next point I should like to make by way of general observation at this stage is that in making the subdivisions and establishing categories of murder, capital and noncapital, we have avoided the rigid classifications which are found in the 1957 homicide act passed in the United Kingdom. Of course, it may well be a proper subject of debate in this committee whether or not we have erred in making that decision, but we made it after analysing all the evidence which was available for study, all the opinions of statements of authority, and after looking at the effect of the United Kingdom act and reading the evidence of deep public soul searching which is going on in Great Britain now as a result of some of the consequences of their homicide act. After this study we came to the conclusion that the type of division. applicable to the crime of murder should not be made on the basis applied in the United Kingdom because a division of that kind has produced some unfortunate results, some of which I outlined previously but which will yet bear repetition. The most glaring deficiency is, of course, that when a distinction between capital and non-capital murder is made on the basis of the weapon with which the murder was committed, or the person or class of person killed, instead of the nature and circumstances of the crime itself, as we have done, a situation is produced in which the public is bound to be concerned about the results which follow. For example, if a man kills with a gun he is liable to the death penalty but if he kills with a club or by strangulation he is not liable to the death penalty.
In our view the proper course is to look at the character and circumstances of the crime itself and to ask the jury to inquire of itself whether the murder was planned and deliberate or not. The decision rests on the answer of that question. It does not seem to

us that a killing with a gun is any the less reprehensible; it is still an act of supreme defiance of society's basic law, as serious as an act of killing with some other weapon. It is, surely, the act of killing which constitutes the offence and whether or not that killing was planned and deliberate rather than the means by which it was accomplished.
The other point that I wish to make of a general nature arises in connection with the suggestion that consideration of this bill be suspended or postponed and the bill itself referred to a special committee.

Mr. Chairman, I will come to that question when I deal with the remarks made by the hon. gentleman who has just asked it. Obviously he was under a misapprehension as to the import of those words. I should point out, as I will in detail when I deal with his remarks, that the words "- in respect of any person-" taken in context with the subsequent words, "-on the part of such person-" make it clear that the person referred to is the person who commits the crime and not the person killed. I shall enlarge upon that when I come to the hon. member's criticism, which it seemed to me at the time, was made on the basis of a misapprehension as to the effect of those words.
The suggestion has been made, and repeated in several quarters, that we should interrupt our consideration and postpone our study, and that the bill be referred to a special committee of the house. Those who made this suggestion have done so on the unjustified and erroneous assumptions that this bill has been hastily and badly drafted, without proper study on the part of the government, or the government officials who drafted it, and that it has been presented to the house in circumstances, as it were, when the house has neither had previous opportunity to consider the matter, nor has a present opportunity to give it fullest study. Every one of those assumptions is, of course, completely erroneous.
Furthermore, the suggestion is made, on an equally erroneous assumption, that somehow or other, the procedure followed in the United Kingdom was different, and their homicide act, whether we agree with it or not, was produced and enacted as a result of the fullest and most detailed study of the particular proposals contained therein. Nothing could be further from the truth, nor further from the case. The British homicide act was not only

Criminal Code
not referred to a special committee of parliament, it was not before the Gowers royal commission and, indeed, in most of its particulars, it departed from the recommendations of the Gowers commission. The proposals contained in the British homicide act were never before the Gowers commission for its study or consideration.

They could not refrain, unless they refused to answer every question they were asked, from expressing a view which might well be in variance with what parliament decided to do. Royal commissions do not enact laws, parliament does. So, it is quite a different thing to have a judge give the benefit of his opinion and experience to a royal commission which is charged with making recommendations, from the situation which would arise if judges expressed their opinions in respect of proposals which were then before parliament, on the verge of being translated into law, and which would then later be before those judges for interpretation and application.
Mr. Chairman, this brings me to a consideration of some of the specific points that 90205-6-350
have been made by hon. members in the course of the discussion here today. The hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanau-diere made a suggestion that the French version at least should be amended to include the word "prepare", in addition to the words "projete" and "delibere". I would never claim to be a sufficient scholar of French, or the meaning of the French language, to be able to say whether the two words "projete" and "delibere" properly and completely transport into the French language the meaning of the words "planned" and "deliberate", as they are contained in the English text. This is a matter in respect of which we are in the hands of the translators and experts in that field. That certainly was the intention of the hon. member's remarks. I would be very reluctant to say that one or the other version goes any further than the words "planned" and "deliberate", so that I can only say we will take the matter under advisement. As the hon. member knows, we have, in the ranks of my colleagues not only experts in the use of the French language, but a very real expert in criminal law in the person of my colleague the Secretary of State. We will take the matter under advisement and, if we consider the words now used in the French text do not properly carry into effect the meaning that is intended in the English text, we shall give further consideration to the matter.
This morning the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont said first that, as a result of this legislation, capital punishment, although preserved in words, would really become a museum piece. I do not think I need comment on that suggestion further than I have in the course of my general remarks made a few moments ago, when I presented, as my view, that juries would not be unable to answer the simple question as to whether or not a killing was planned and deliberate, and that if a jury came to an affirmative conclusion, it would then be unable or unwilling to bring in a verdict accordingly. The hon. member, it seemed to me, in the course of his remarks in respect of clause 1, went back to his objection to the principle of the bill, and his whole approach was based on the objection to the division of murder into capital and noncapital murder. In that regard I can only say that I am unable to satisfy him because, in our view, which is a view shared by the majority of the members of this committee including, as he knows, members of his own party, murder should be divided into capital and non-capital murder.
The hon. member went on to say, at one point in his remarks, that all changes made

Criminal Code
in the United Kingdom were made as a result of intensive study on the part of jurists and others. He was joined by the hon. member for Essex East in the suggestion that we should refer this measure to a parliamentary committee before which we should invite these experts, including jurists and others. I have already expressed my view that it would be entirely inappropriate to invite judges to come before such a committee. I have already expressed, in general terms, my satisfaction, that this bill and the subject matter with which it deals, have received the fullest and most complete study in this country, in this parliament, and by this parliament, to the point where we are now able to perform our duties in dealing with a specific proposal. I do not think there is any element of parliament being taken by surprise, or being unprepared, and we feel this bill should be proceeded with at this time in this committee.
May I point out again, however, that a comparison of what was done in the United Kingdom, with what is being done here, indicates that my hon. friends, who make the suggestion, have completely failed to understand what did happen there. They suggest that the change the United Kingdom made in the homicide act of 1957 was handled something along the lines of the suggestion they make. Bear in mind first that the United Kingdom bill, as it passed through their parliament, in its major effect rejects the recommendations of the Gowers commission. The Gowers commission was set up in 1949 and it reported in 1953. It did not have before it any specific proposal. Its terms of reference were:
To consider and report whether liability under the criminal law in Great Britain to sutler capital punishment for murder should be limited or modified.
That is all they had before them, the question of principle, not of detailed legislation. As I say, the commission made its report in 1953. it was not until 1957 that the government of the United Kingdom introduced legislation to deal with the matter, and the legislation that was brought in was based not on the Gowers commission report or on any other long and extensive study of a specific proposal. But in so far as its division of murder into degrees or types which carry the death penalty and life imprisonment respectively is concerned, it was based almost entirely on a proposal which was made by eight private members on the government side. That bill was introduced-I am not at all being critical of what was done, I am confining my remarks to a report on the facts-and in that respect, as I say, it originated from a very small group but, however, it did carry the judgment of the House of

Commons and the House of Lords. It was passed without any lengthy or extraordinarily lengthy debate. It was not referred to any special or standing committee of the House of Commons; it was treated in the ordinary way. It went through first and second readings, committee of the whole and third reading.
On the other hand, when you come to consider what has happened in Canada, what this bill deals with is the carrying into effect of a decision in principle on the question of whether murder should be divided into degrees. In Canada we have had exhaustive consideration by a parliamentary committee of both houses which sat in 1954 and 1955; in other words, for two years. It is true it also considered corporal punishment and lotteries, but it devoted extensive consideration to the question of capital punishment, whether it should be abolished and whether the law of murder should be changed. It heard a large number of experts on this question, and we have had the benefit of the evidence given before that committee, of the report of that committee and of its conclusions.
In addition, in this house for two years now this matter has been debated as well as being discussed and considered intensely by members outside this chamber. Therefore, it is completely erroneous to suggest that this subject comes as a new one to the members of the house, or that there has not been given to the subject the fullest and most ample consideration on the basis of which not only the government but the members are now in possession of every argument that could be advanced on either side, and are as fully as they will ever be in a position to make up their minds on the merits or otherwise of the specific proposal now laid before them. Therefore I can see no purpose whatsoever to be served under those circumstances, which are quite different from the circumstances surrounding the discussion of the bill of rights, in delaying the passage of this bill and referring it to a special committee.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont said that after all it is not so important, there is lots of time, it would not hurt even if it did mean delay. The hon. member for Niagara Falls also posed certain questions. Incidentally, I might remind the committee that she has had considerable experience in the field of criminal law and has acted as defence counsel or participated in murder trials in more than one instance. She asked me what would be the situation if there was a riot in a prison during which there was an unpremeditated killing and her suggestion was that there is nothing in the bill that would make this capital murder. The Leader of the Opposition asked the same question. To this I can only reply that it would be difficult, it seems to me, to envisage such a case where it did not take place either in the course of an effort to escape or to effect a rescue from prison in which case it would be covered under section 202 or, alternatively, where it would be possible to establish that on the part of the person who actually did the killing the act of killing itself was planned and deliberate. I, of course, do not attempt to lay down an answer for every conceivable case that might arise but in our view the killing of a prison officer is covered in the provisions for capital murder.
The hon. lady also asked me what the situation would be with respect to a second killing. Again, we have made our division of murder into capital and non-capital on the basis of whether or not the killing was planned and deliberate or carried out in the course of committing any of the crimes or offences covered in section 202. That is the principle which we carry forward. That is the principle which we would hope and expect that juries would apply to every case of killing that comes before them. As I say, in the drafting of the legislation we have in our view protected the situation with regard to the type of murder involved in the killing of a prison officer or a police or peace officer.
She also asked me why we had not accepted and incorporated into the bill the doctrine of diminished responsibility. I should point out to her that both the Gowers commission and our own parliamentary committee recommended against the importation into Canadian law of this doctrine of diminished responsibility.
Again, the question was asked whether or not, if a mentally retarded person was persuaded, encouraged and, indeed, led by a person in full control of his faculties into committing a robbery in a bank in the course of which he armed himself and killed, that would be capital murder. That, of course, would depend upon whether the person in full possession of his mental faculties counselled

or procured the doing of the act which resulted in the death. On the basis of the general outline of the case presented by the hon. lady, I would say that the probability would be that the jury would find that the other person did so counsel or procure so as to make it capital murder, but again it would be a question to be determined on the basis of the facts.
The hon. member for Nickel Belt criticized us because he said we had no public document to substantiate the views of the government as incorporated in the bill. On an earlier occasion and again this afternoon I have endeavoured to summarize the process by which we arrived at our decision in principle. We did so after a review of the Gowers commission report, our own parliamentary committee's report, the vast volume of other writings and speeches on the subject, debates in this house and views as expressed in the country. On the basis of that study and analysis we reached our decision in principle as to what we should do, which was that we should divide murder into two categories, capital and non-capital. Accordingly we have produced a bill which carries that into effect and we now bring it before the house for the judgment of the house.
We are prepared to defend the decision we have made both in general and in detail. As I have said, surely after all these years the House of Commons is in a position now where it is appropriate that it should be asked to make up its mind on the question of how it wants to deal with murder. It did happen in the past, I think-my little experience does not allow me to prove it-but I suppose it did happen in some cases that people, having been found guilty, were put to death though they were innocent. This is the sort of thing we must try to avoid.
I do not wish at this time to follow the Prime Minister of this country in the statement he made this afternoon and take up all those reasons after him to comment on them or criticize them.

Mr. Chairman, in spite of the attitude which the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice took this afternoon, I still believe, like others who spoke before me, that this bill should be submitted to a special committee. It is true that a joint committee of the house and of the other place did some work with regard to this matter in 1954 and in 1955. It is also true, as I said earlier, that the bill was discussed last year, but, here in this house, we are called upon to take the best possible decision. Notwithstanding the position taken by the minister, I think that in order to arrive at the best possible decision, we must make the best use of whatever means are afforded by the rules of this house to form our opinion.
We want opinions freely expressed and to this end we should exhaust all means of persuasion trying to drive home the merit of this bill and, for the moment, that of the first clause.
I am a lawyer myself, as are many members of this house. However, several members have not had experience in court. I am sure too that none of my colleagues have ever known what it was to be indicted or to serve as a juryman.
During my short legal career, I have had occasion to defend a person accused of murder. An attorney is always in a difficult situation in such cases whether he acts for the crown or for the defence. That is why parliament and the committee must take every possible means within the purview of the rules to arrive at a sound and logical decision.
I feel that the best way to make this measure as efficient as possible would be to refer the bill and clause 1 to a special committee.

Too often, in the past, individuals were charged with murder and convicted of murder, while they should have been convicted of manslaughter. Too often also individuals were prosecuted for manslaughter when the proper charge should have been one of murder. I think that danger is being warded off by the definition of capital murder and non-capital murder found in clause 1 of this bin. I do not mean by that that I am personally satisfied with the classes as described in clause 1. Far from that. As I have just pointed out, the law now provides for cases of murder and manslaughter. Perhaps it might be useful, in making my point, to recall that murder is the intentional act of killing, of voluntarily taking the life of another person, while manslaughter or unintentional homicide is the involuntary act, although culpable, of taking the life of another person.

This bill includes capital and non-capital murders, manslaughter or unintentional culpable homicide remaining as described in our statutes.

We have accordingly started on the basis that there are two broad types of killing. The first is where the death does not result from any act of deliberation on the part of the person causing it but can be said to be Impulsive or non-deliberate, in the sense of being in no way within the prior contemplation of that person. It is our view that the death penalty ought not to be the consequence in these cases, and accordingly although the crime may be murder, it is classed as non-capital and a sentence of life imprisonment only is provided.
The other type of killing is the case where death is caused deliberately or as a result of a planned act of the person causing it. All these cases are classed as capital murder and for these cases, but for these cases only, the sentence of death will follow automatically on conviction.

While it is true that the judiciary is there to interpret the law, it is also true that the lawmakers are here to make the laws as clear as possible. I therefore think that from that point of view, it is important to look into the definition of the words. With respect to the word "delibere", here is the meaning given to this word in its adjectival form by the Larousse dictionary:
-easy, free, determined-

Then the dictionary gives an example:
By deliberate intent, with intention, purposely.
Now here is what is meant, according to the French dictionary, by the verb "deliberer":
To consult together, to reflect inwardly for the purpose of reaching a decision.
And I stress this part of the definition of the verb:

deliberate,-

In my opinion, both dictionaries do not give the same definition and I do not think we can rely on any other source of information than dictionaries for the definition or the meaning of words. Now, the English word "deliberate" seems to imply a more or less lengthy period of time which is certainly not only an instant, while the French word "delibere" does not seem to make such a distinction. Indeed, I think it is possible to deliberate only one second and, in such a case, murder still is deliberate.
I will now go a little further. If it is true that a homicide must be deliberate to be considered as a murder under the present law, the same thing can be said about the bill under consideration.
In my opinion, the word "deliberate" in the English version implies lengthy and planned deliberation, a debate within the criminal's mind, if you wish, whereas the word "deliberation" as defined by French dictionaries could mean reflection which took only a flick of an instant.
Is it possible, however, to separate the words "planned" and "deliberate" used in the bill? That is why I was pointing out a while ago that when the minister was speaking about "planned and deliberate" murder, this afternoon, he was coupling the two words every time he used the expression.
If, after having decided to kill someone, I plan my deed and then I carry it out, it
Criminal Code
is obvious that the homicide I have committed is deliberate; however, I could have taken a decision after hasty deliberation, without any preconceived plan. In that case, is it a capital or a non-capital murder? This question has been haunting me all day long.
Nowhere have I heard an appropriate answer but it seems, at first sight, that to have a capital murder, it should be both "planned" and "deliberate", whereas if it is simply a "deliberate" and not a "planned" murder, you have non-capital murder.
