Mr. Chairman, I rise at this time to make one or two comments on the first clause of this bill. Since I have been interested in capital punishment I have already put my views on the record by the introduction of a bill based on the United Kingdom legislation but adapted to Canadian conditions. I agree with the minister in the adoption and the adaptation of the principles expressed in this legislation, but I feel this is the time for the committee to do the final polishing of the words placed before us which seek to put the principles into legislative expression.
In his introductory remarks on capital punishment the minister indicated that generally speaking he believed it was a deterrent to rational people. He also left the logical implication that those who find themselves in the unfortunate position of having committed capital murder are in the circle of what one could call irrational people by the very fact that they find themselves in this position. If we assume then the premise that those people who find themselves in the position of having committed capital murder are in varying degrees irrational, I think it requires an extremely close examination to find out which people within that circle are the ones the court decides shall suffer the supreme penalty. My own feeling on this particular matter, Mr. Chairman, is that I should like to approach the problem from a slightly different direction.
We have indicated positively what the crime consists of by saying that it must be planned and deliberate. In order to delineate very carefully what the words "planned and deliberate" mean we have to give consideration to some of the defences advanced, such as insanity and drunkenness. The first one I shall more particularly deal with is the defence of insanity. Under section 16 of the Criminal Code we are still operating basically under M'Naghten's rule, which described legal insanity. This rule is now some 118 years old. I am concerned with whether or not during this whole period of 118 years this rule has been entirely effective. We are faced first with the medical aspects of insanity which are far ahead of the legal understanding of the situation. I am very much concerned over this gap. It is particularly important, Mr. Chairman, because mens rea is the prime ingredient required to prove a capital murder case. In the United States in 1954, in a case called the Durham case, they attempted to define much more clearly the psychoses and neuroses of insanity which would lead to the crime being committed. I 	.
suggest that under the present criminal legislation here there is not the same degree of flexibility that they have in the United States.
My first suggestion to the minister would be-although this is perhaps not the appropriate time to do it-that consideration be given to setting up a committee to study insanity both from the juridical and medical point of view with a view to up-dating the sections which deal at present with legal insanity.
The second point that I should like to deal with, Mr. Chairman, is the fact that in a capital murder case the death penalty is prescribed in section 642 of the Criminal Code. In prescribing the death penalty, I would suggest that the penalty and the method are inextricably interwoven. I have already gone on record and suggested that a suitable method of the death penalty is the gas chamber. The hon. member for Essex East and the Leader of the Opposition both indirectly raised this matter by suggesting that perhaps there should be another form of capital punishment.

There is another point I wish to make briefly before I sit down. It seems to me, as has been indicated by other members who have spoken, that the two key words in the clause are "planned" and "deliberate". In the light of the definitions I have been able to find I am wondering about the necessity for the use of the word "planned" and whether the word "and" is likely to be judicially interpreted as "or". In trying to find a definition of the word "deliberate" the only success I had was in Black's Law Dictionary, fourth edition. The cases referred to are United States cases but I suggest that the reasoning would probably be equally as applicable to Canadian courts. I quote part of the definition of "deliberate" as found on page 513:
By the use of this word, in describing a crime, the idea is conveyed that the perpetrator weighs the motives for the act and its consequences, the nature of the crime, or other things connected with his intentions, with a view to a decision thereon; that he carefully considers all these; and that the act is not suddenly committed. It implies that the perpetrator must be capable of the exercise of such mental powers as are called into use by deliberation and the consideration and weighing of motives and consequences.
Using that particular definition, it appears to me that the idea of planning or something having been planned is incorporated. Perhaps I might read one more definition that is given here:
"Deliberation" and "premeditation" are of the same character of mental operations, differing only-in degree. Deliberation is but prolonged premeditation. In other words, in law, deliberation is premeditation in a cool state of the blood, or, where there has been heat of passion, it is premeditation continued beyond the period within which there has been time for the blood to cool, in the given case. Deliberation is not only to think of beforehand, which may be but for an instant, but the inclination to do the act is considered, weighed, pondered upon, for such a length of time after a provocation is given as the jury may find was sufficient for the blood to cool. One in a heat of passion may premeditate without deliberating. Deliberation is only exercised in a cool state of the blood, while premeditation may be either in that state of the blood or in the heat of passion.
Incidentally, I think this might also answer the question raised by the hon. member for York-Scarborough who wanted the idea of cold-bloodedness included so that it could be said that it was a planned, deliberate and coldblooded murder. I think this definition clearly incorporates under "deliberate" the idea of cold-bloodedness. On a very cursory examination, it does not appear to me that the word "planned" is necessary. I wonder whether the minister would give this point careful consideration because although I am making these criticisms I do so on the basis that it is our task in this committee to produce the best possible legislation covering these particular points. Mr. Chairman, several hon. members have suggested that I should attempt to define the words "planned and deliberate" as used in this clause. I think there is very great danger in attempting such a definition precisely because, as I have said, in the final analysis the courts interpret and are the proper authorities to interpret the words of a statute. Of course, in considering the import of words it must be realized that their applications-not their meaning but their application-will vary from case to case depending upon the circumstances of that case. The evidence of what took place has to be weighed and the jury, subject to direction from the judge, will then have to apply their minds to whether or not the circumstances in that case show that there was a planned and deliberate murder.
However, I have no objection to indicating the concept that we worked out and have asked the experts to incorporate into the technical language of a bill. The purpose of using the expression "planned and deliberate" was to add something to the usual idea of intent or mens rea or malice aforethought. That something is an element of greater premeditation than the expressions I have mentioned necessarily connote. Because the words "deliberate and premeditated" in the United States have tended in some states to be equated to mere intent, we selected words which in our view would and do make plain that something more than intent formed on the spur of the moment and under a sudden passion or impulse is required to constitute capital murder. So it will be appreciated that instead of using the words "deliberate and premeditated" we have used the words "planned and deliberate" in order to give expression to the thought that something more than mere intent or mens rea or malice aforethought, as they have been interpreted, is involved.
We all know the meaning of "planned" and of "deliberate". They import the idea of the mind making and carrying out a project not thrust upon it by sudden passion or impulse. I think a time element is present but it may vary from case to case. Plans may be conceived and carried out very quickly but they must be plans and not merely impulses. When the words are applied to a specific set of facts, as they always will be in practice, I do not think a judge will have too much trouble explaining or a jury understand the definition. Finally, I suggest that "deliberate" has no direct bearing on the question of mental capacity, which remains as it is now.

We have also, Mr. Chairman, given some consideration to the point raised first by the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere and referred to recently by the hon. member for Megantic, namely, the question of whether or not the French translation, "projete et delibere", did carry into effective language the concept I have outlined as the concept involved in the English words, "planned and deliberate". It has been suggested to me that possibly they do not as accurately reflect the concept as those words in the English text. It will be appreciated, as I said earlier, that this is a very technical question, the determination of whether or not certain words or certain phrases in French have exactly the same meaning in that language as phrases or words in the English language. I am not in the least qualified to express an opinion on this matter, and I would normally be guided entirely by the opinion of the translators who are trained in this work.
However, after some discussion I am advised that it may well be conceded that the words "planned and deliberate" in English would be better rendered or rather the concept of that phrase would be better rendered by the French words "projete et premedite" rather than the words "projete et delibere." I am informed, too, that the French word "premedite" used in this context does not have the rather restricted meaning of the English word "premeditated" as it has been interpreted judicially. We would be quite prepared, therefore, to consider substitution of the words "projete et premedite" for the words "projete et delibere."
There is only one other comment I should like to make in connection with this clause, in response to a suggestion made by hon. members in connection with the position of prison officers and police officers. I believe it was the hon. member for Niagara Falls who first raised the question of whether the killing of a prison officer in the course of a riot where the purpose of the riot was not directly to escape or effect rescue from the prison but was, shall we say, in the course of protest against conditions in the prison, would be considered capital murder. The hon. member suggested that an inmate acting on impulse might kill a guard, and asked would that be capital murder. I ventured the suggestion earlier this afternoon that it would probably be regarded as capital murder, one or the other of the two types of capital murder, namely as a killing committed in the course of an attempt to escape or effect a rescue, or as a planned and deliberate murder. In the case of an inmate, particularly one who may have smuggled a

weapon into the prison, and then used it in the course of a riot, a killing with it would very likely result in a jury finding that the killing was planned and deliberate under those circumstances. I do, however, want to make clear that it was our intention to cover such circumstances. It is our view that by reference to those offences under section 202, plus the provision regarding a planned and deliberate carrying out of murder, such a case is covered as being capital murder. However, lest there be any doubt on the matter I will be quite prepared to consider an amendment to add a specific provision making it clear that the killing of a prison officer by an inmate in those circumstances is capital murder because that would not change the intent with which we started out in this bill. Similarly, in so far as the killing of a police officer in the course of his duty is concerned, that situation might be specifically covered also. I am not suggesting here a final drafting of such an amendment. I believe these situations are covered now because section 202 refers to a killing in the course of resisting lawful arrest. I think in most circumstances where one could envisage a person killing a police officer, the police officer would be acting in the course of his duty and the situation would, therefore, come under that general coverage.
As I have said, it is our intention that these situations should be included. However, I understand that several hon. members of experience are concerned, so I see no harm in making it perfectly clear by a special reference to both the position of the prison officer and the police officer, and we will be glad to consider the drafting of such a provision.

It was because of the action of juries and, as the minister pointed out, some enlightened bankers a little later on, that finally pressure was brought to bear which reduced the application of the death penalty at that time.

If through this bill we put into the hands of the jury the additional question of fact, as the minister expressed it earlier today, of determining as a matter of fact whether a murder is planned and deliberate, it seems to me we should perhaps use language which will have a more complete meaning to a jury.
I suggested last week, when the discussion in committee first began, that perhaps "coldblooded" might be another adjective to add to the description that in my view the majority of people in this country have in mind. I have selected and discarded a number of other words since that time and have come up with two specific suggestions, that a murder to qualify as capital murder should be vicious, cold-blooded, planned and deliberate.
To support that suggestion I offer on the one hand the suggestion that words to persons who must, to qualify for jury duty, be not learned in the law will carry a different sort of weight than the rather confining language of law generally. It seems to me that juries will be able to better understand the implications of the words "vicious and cold-blooded" than the simpler words "planned and deliberate" that are proposed at the present time.
I offer as one of the few examples an editorial in the Toronto Telegram of May 16, 1961, where the caption is "Murder in cold blood". In other words, it seems to me that is what we must have in this law, if we are handing over so much more responsibility to juries. Like the hon. member for Parkdale and other hon. members, I have great confidence in the jury system and certainly the way in which this system has been responsible for various reforms in connection with capital punishment over the years.
It seems to me that the question at the top rung of the ladder, if you like, should include a more precise and generally better understood description of what I believe this parliament had in mind in describing the type of murder for which capital punishment should be the penalty and what I am very confident is in the minds of the majority of Canadians who have expressed their opinions on this matter on a continuing basis in recent years. I do not know at what point I should move this form of amendment, but perhaps now is as good a time as any.
I should like to go on to ask what is, perhaps, a layman's question about the word "or". I wonder whether the minister could answer this question before I proceed. In clause 1 (2) (a) it is said:
it is planned and deliberate on the part of such person, or
Then you go on to subclause (b). It seems to me there might be some merit in changing that word "or" to "and", and perhaps the

minister would point out the reason for the use of the word "or" rather than the word "and".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
The use of the word "or" there is appropriate because it is our intention to make these alternatives. Therefore the conjunction "or" is used rather than the conjunction "and" because if "and" were used you would have to prove that the murder had both these elements; in other words, that not only was it planned and deliberate but also that the killing took place in the course of the commission or the attempted commission of another crime. This to us is not at all appropriate.
The crime in mind may have been the crime of murder, which has no relation at all to any other crime. Therefore we do not want to provide that capital murder must have both elements. All we want to provide is that capital murder is a killing which is itself planned or deliberate, or a killing which occurs in the course of committing other crimes which by their nature import not only an element of violence and, as it were, defiance of society, but also the element of deliberation; that is, the person embarked on a course of deliberation, stealth or violence and in the course of carrying it out he killed. In our view that imports the element of deliberation which we feel should be present to constitute capital murder.
We do not intend to provide, and it would be a mistake to provide, that not only must the killing itself be planned and deliberate but it must take place in the course of the commission of another offence in order to be capital murder. That would be the effect if we used the word "and" instead of "or".

Killing by an explosive such as a bomb is surely covered by the general provision regarding deliberate or planned murder. For example, if anyone successfully plants a bomb in a plane he surely cannot be thought to be guilty of anything other than a planned and deliberate killing. Similarly, if the accused plants a bomb somewhere on the surface of the earth that could only be a planned and deliberate killing, we felt it was not necessary to broaden the definition of "weapon" so as to take care of that case.

I appreciate the point the minister made concerning the rigidity of the system which might be imposed on the provincial authorities by the establishment of boards of psychiatrists, but I have had some experience of the problem caused by psychiatric evidence while I was acting in the capacity of a juror. I recall that during one trial the prisoner apparently went to sleep in the dock. An issue then arose which assumed the form of a trial within a trial. The defence argued to the effect that if a man could fall asleep in a courtroom when he was on trial for his life this was prima facie evidence of insanity of some sort. We heard some learned argument on both sides for and against this proposition. We then retired to the jury room in this trial within a trial, as I have said, to decide the question whether the accused was really asleep or whether he was only pretending to be asleep. This was an interesting diversion, but how can any group of persons looking at another person decide whether in fact that person is asleep or pretending to be asleep? Since there was no conclusive evidence it was virtually impossible to decide. However, we came to the conclusion that since the matter of insanity would be arising later in any event we would decide, for the time being at any rate, that there was a possibility of malingering. But after the psychiatrists had confronted the jury-and this jury was made up of persons from many walks of life with various backgrounds, degrees of education and vocabulary-by the time we had heard the psychiatric evidence presented by both sides, members of the jury quite frankly were more confused than before the presentation of this psychiatric evidence.
Having had that experience, coupled with the opinion expressed in different articles which I have read along this line, I have come to the conclusion that the hon. member for Charlevoix may be right in his suggestion regarding the establishment of such a board.
I should also like to state that the minister has not acknowledged-perhaps he does not agree-that there are findings within the application of the M'Naghten rule, which should apply, nor has he given any reason why a clause, similar to the diminished responsibility clause in the British act, should not be inserted into this proposed new legislation. He did say earlier this afternoon that a recommendation to include such a clause was not put forth by either the Gowers commission or our parliamentary committee. With great respect, however, I would submit that is not a powerful argument for its exclusion, because the principles included in this bill itself are not included either in the Gowers
commission recommendations or the recommendations put forward by the Canadian parliamentary committee.

Mr. Chairman, I am not quite sure I appreciate the point the hon. member for York-Scarborough is trying to make. I do not know whether he is referring to the desirability of having the examination of a person, who has been sentenced to death, carried out by a board of psychiatrists, or referring to the desirability of examining every person who faces a capital murder charge, carried out by a board of psychiatrists. If he is referring to the desirability of having every person examined by a psychiatrist, that person having been sentenced to death, I should remind him of the practice which has been, for many years, and is being carried out, of having a psychiatrist retained by the federal government examine persons in precisely those circumstances. The cabinet receives a full report from that psychiatrist, which is available to it in its consideration of the question of exercising clemency.
We have one psychiatrist for all English speaking Canadians who journeys around the country examining persons sentenced to death. There is another psychiatrist who examines all French speaking individuals who are similarly condemned. We obtain adequate and thorough consideration in respect of the psychiatric condition of condemned men in this way, as well as a degree of uniformity in approach, which I think is most desirable in these cases. In addition, of course, any psychiatric evidence given at the trial is available to the cabinet, and it is the practice of the federal government psychiatrists to consult, generally speaking, with others who have given psychiatric evidence, if that individual feels that consultation is helpful.
With regard to the doctrine of diminished responsibility, I realize that views vary, but I should like to refer to this question again, if for no other reason than to correct a misstatement I made this afternoon. I believe I said that both the Gowers commission, of the United Kingdom, and our own parliamentary committee had made recommendations against the adoption of that doctrine. To be completely accurate, I should have said that the Gowers commission recommended against the importation of this law into England, although it said it had no objection to its application as then incorporated in the law of Scotland. It did, however, recommend against its extension. In Canada it was not our parliamentary committee which made the recommendation against it, because it did not deal with the subject at all. The royal commission on the law of insanity recommended, as found

at page 46 of their report, conclusion No. 11, against the adoption of the law of diminished responsibility in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to make a few more remarks concerning this proposed legislation, prompted by the remarks made by the Prime Minister this afternoon, as well as by the fact that the Minister of Justice has involuntarily omitted to comment on a remark which I made concerning paragraph (i) 1, or 1 (i).
The Prime Minister made it quite clear by his remarks this afternoon that he felt something should be done in Canada to assure that no one who was convicted on circumstantial evidence of the crime of murder, or any other crime, should lose his life because of it. This feeling is shared by most hon. members of this house, as well as the majority of citizens of Canada. However, I felt the Prime Minister was blowing both hot and cold, because as clause 1 of this proposed measure now exists, there is no effort represented there, on the part of the government, to pass a law which would prevent the conviction and execution of any individual on solely circumstantial evidence. One always realizes the horror of the situation when a man is sentenced to death, because there is always the possibility that an innocent man will lose his life. In spite of this fact, and the words of the Prime Minister this afternoon, we find nowhere in this bill, as presented to us at this time, a clause representing any effort on the part of the government, to eradicate the possibility of such a thing taking place. I suggest that many people in this country, and more specifically a judge, with whom I recently spoke, have objection to the present law, which is not changed substantially by this bill, in this respect, because it does not include a high degree of security or safeguard, so that individuals in this country will not be convicted or hanged on circumstantial evidence. While I must admit there is no portion of
Criminal Code
this bill which deals with the subject, clause 1 does attempt to segregate crimes in respect of which capital punishment applies. This is one problem for which there is no solution contained in this bill.
As one reads clause 1 one sees that something is being done to try to do away with capital punishment by the back door. If clause 1 is passed in the form in which it now reads, murder in Canada will from now on be punished by life imprisonment, with certain exceptions. This may be of interest to certain hon. members who have made quite a plea for the retention of capital punishment up to a certain point. The punishment for murder in Canada from now on will be life imprisonment except for the offences enumerated in clause 1. I feel there should be two ways of referring to it, namely capital murder and non-capital murder. It seems to me we could retain the phraseology that murder is punishable by life imprisonment and upon a verdict of capital murder being found the penalty is death. This would solve the problem.
I make these remarks with the reservation that it is my opinion that clause 7 should be removed. If clause 7 disappears from this bill there would be no point in enumerating both capital murder and non-capital murder. To introduce the new terminology a verdict of capital murder would suffice.
As I have said, I rose to speak again because the minister-I know he is a busy man -did not answer my remarks on clause (2)(i). I have had occasion to discuss this question with other people learned in the law. They have indicated to me that the responsibility of the accomplice is not the same in clause (2)(i) as in clause (lXii) and (iii). This means that if the crime of murder is committed by hitting a person with an object the accomplice has a greater responsibility for the crime and could be found guilty of murder in such cases much more readily than in other cases such as choking or stopping a person's breath, where the act is repeated. We do not find in clause (l)(i) any reference to the stopping of a person's breath. The clause stops abruptly after the simple words "assisted in causing the bodily harm from which death ensued". This does not necessarily mean assisted in applying force which caused the bodily harm and which itself was the cause of stopping the breath. I feel sure the minister will see my point. I suggest that after the words "assisted in causing the bodily harm" in clause (lXi), there should be added the words "assisted in applying the force causing bodily harm". The physical act of stopping the breath or administering

the stupefying thing would place the accomplice under the same degree of responsibility. I feel the minister should have no objection to this.
The minister tried to answer my query about paragraph (a) which deals with a person who has been killed but not the person who has committed the offence. I realize that the intention of the minister and of parliament is undoubtedly to amend the code so that the person who commits the offence is the person who is referred to. If a murder is a capital offence if the person committing it has deliberately done so, why not say it? Why use the phrase "in respect of any person"? When the reference is to the person committing the offence, why say "in respect of any person" in an important clause such as this? For this reason alone I am still prepared to say that it is an ambiguous clause and that lawyers will debate it and will say that the murder must be deliberate as to the person who is killed. If he kills the wrong person you cannot hang the person committing the offence, particularly if he can be found guilty of committing another type of murder. I repeat, the clause is ambiguous. I say that I might construe the meaning to be the opposite of that which the minister would give to it. Why does he not use the words "the person who committed" and let us be done with it? Mr. Chairman, sub-section 2(a) of clause 1 of the bill gives me some concern. I do not know whether this point was raised before, as I was not in the house in the early part of the evening, but I have reference to the use of the conjunction "and" between the words "planned" and "deliberate". I do not consider these two words as being synonymous. The word "planned", I think, does not admit of much doubt as to its meaning. I think any murder which is planned must be deliberate, that is, the killing must follow as a deliberate act. But I do not think that a murder which is deliberate need have been planned. I think there is a distinction. May I refer to the considered remarks of the minister when he introduced the bill. As found on page 5223 of Hansard, he said:
In carrying out the delicate but important task of bringing the law into line with our convictions in this field, we have concentrated our attention on producing a system which represents a rational and logical application of those principles of law upon which I have touched. We have accordingly started on the basis that there are two broad types of killing. The first is where the death does not result from any act of deliberation on the part of the person causing it-
At that point I wish to note that the word "planned" was not used.
-but can be said to be impulsive or nondeliberate, in the sense of being in no way within the prior contemplation of that person. It is our
Criminal Code
view that the death penalty ought not to be the consequence in these cases, and accordingly although the crime may be murder, it is classed as non-capital and a sentence of life imprisonment only is provided.
I point out, Mr. Chairman, that the view expressed there was that in order for the murder to be classed as non-capital it must be impulsive and non-deliberate and no reference is made to the fact that it must not be planned. The minister went on to say:
The other type of killing is the case where death is caused deliberately-
Then the word "or" is used.
-or as the result of a planned act of the person causing it. All these cases are classed as capital murder and for these cases, but for these cases only, the sentence of death will follow automatically on conviction.
My desire is that an explanation be given why the word "or" should not be used instead of the conjunction "and" because from the explanation given by the minister it appears to me that there are such things as murders which, in the one case, are deliberate and murders which, in the other case, are both deliberate and previously planned.
I think it might be of importance to read another paragraph which follows a little further on in which reference is made to the second type of murder. The minister said:
The second is the category in which, although a killing itself may not have been consciously and initially planned, yet the course of action embarked upon or planned had within it such an element of criminality and violence, as well as of deliberation or stealth, that the killing must properly be regarded-
Then, I emphasize these words:
-as deliberate by the person who did it or who counselled or procured the doing of the act which caused it.
These words, of course, have reference to paragraph (b) of subclause 2 which deals with murders which fall within section 202. In the case of these murders, you will note that it is capital murder where death follows the commission or the attempt to commit certain definite offences. The deaths that ensue need not be planned or deliberate. The deaths result during the commission of the offences and if death is caused by an individual, by his own act, then that killing is considered to be capital murder.
My concern is that in the explanation the planning and deliberateness were not considered to be a necessary combination. The deliberateness, in itself, would justify capital punishment, and that was the construction I took from the remarks that were made. If you used deliberateness in the commission of the murder then, that alone, would be sufficient to classify it as capital murder.

Mr. Chairman, a little earlier this evening I gave the committee an outline of the concept we had in mind which we have translated into legal terms by the use of the words "planned and deliberate". I said it was our view that what was necessary was something more than what was usually involved in intent or mens rea or malice aforethought. I pointed out also that the words "deliberate and premeditated" in the United States have tended in some states at any rate to be interpreted as meaning not much more than mens rea or intent as those words are defined in a legal sense. We wanted something more than that.
I would point out a significant passage in the Gowers commission report which draws attention to the fact that in most jurisdictions where there are degrees of murder, the division of the degrees is based on the original enactment of the commonwealth of Pennsylvania which has carried into legal form this concept that murder which is deliberate and premeditated, to use their words, should be capital and other types of murder non-capital. The actual words are that "all murder which shall be perpetrated by means of poison, by lying in wait or by any other kinds of deliberate and premeditated killings are capital murders." As I say, most jurisdictions where this kind of division has been attempted use words based on that definition, and generally the words are "deliberate and premeditated".
We felt, as I say, that while this country would not necessarily follow the pattern of the law of the United States, nevertheless they both spring from common roots and the tendency there has been to narrow the interpretation of "deliberate and premeditated". We wanted, therefore, to find another word that would import an element of something beyond mere intent or mens rea and we felt the words "planned and deliberate" best achieved that purpose. I do not think there can be much argument that something which is deliberate might well not be planned and deliberate in the legal meaning. Somebody might pull a gun and deliberately squeeze the trigger. This may well be the result of an impulse and therefore, in the sense of being a planned murder, would not fall within the definition. As I have tried to indicate, we feel that the words "planned and deliberate", not planned or deliberate, bring in this concept of something more than a mere formation of intent.

Therefore it would appear to the court from the evidence of the birth certificate that the accused is under 18 years of age and there would be no doubt about it. But supposing there were no birth certificate. In that case the matter of the evidence as to his apparent age becomes important.
In that case I think it is important to have this provision, because it may well be that a person who looks to be more than 18 years of age might be shown by other evidence to be not more than 18 or to be under 18. So I think it is important to have this provision in this way. While it is not absolutely conclusive of the matter, I would point out that this is the wording of the corresponding provision in the homicide act of 1957 in the United Kingdom. That provision reads:
Sentence of death shall not be pronounced on or recorded against a person convicted of an offence who appears to the court to have been under the age of 18 years at the time the offence was committed,-

There is in this phrase an opportunity, perhaps by an addition to it, to do something which is in the spirit of the statement made by the minister when he introduced this bill, that is to comply with the feeling which is abroad in the country and the feeling which appears to be agreed upon by most of the members of this committee. It is a simple amendment, but one with far-reaching effects. I have prepared an amendment which in a moment I shall read, and I shall send copies to the minister.
It will be recalled that a parliamentary committee which sat in 1954 and 1955, and of which the minister was a member, at least in 1954, heard several witnesses and, in particular, two, Dr. MacLean of Welland and Mr. Clinton Duffy of California in the United States, and both of them gave evidence gruesome in detail and horrible in concept of different methods of capital punishment. My amendment is to add to the words "shall be sentenced to death" which appear in section 206(1) the following words: "in a central lethal gas chamber".
It goes without saying that the amendment if approved will call for further conseqen-tial amendments by the minister including perhaps the deletion of section 642. I believe this amendment would have the approval of most hon. members and certainly of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond who mentioned this matter an hour or two ago. If we are to retain the death penalty and to accept what the minister has said as to a feeling abroad in the country with respect to capital punishment for some crimes it would appear it is encumbent upon us to ascertain which is the most honourable way of carrying out this sentence-the most efficient way not only of destroying human life but of preserving the body for those to whom it still may have some significance, namely the family, besides being less brutalizing in its effect upon society itself.
It may be noted that I have used the word "central" as a description of the place where the executions are to be carried out. I have had some limited experience of the capital punishment carried out in the county of Welland. It was described by Dr. MacLean in his evidence at page 645 of the report of the special committee of this house and the other place which sat in 1954, and I have had the opportunity to observe the brutalizing effect on members of that community,

not only members of the bar and those associated with the work of the court such as jurymen or employees of the penal system but the public generally which knew that on a certain day within the court house, which is located in the centre of the city, capital punishment would be carried out. Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on clause 2. I was much impressed by the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Bumaby-Richmond who had something to say concerning the use of the simple word "appears" in the clause as proposed. I realize it is a word that is very common in our
[The Chairman.]
courts. The word "appears" is more or less similar to or has the same significance as "finding". I would agree, if the section dealt with the problem which pertained to a finding only which does not cover the appearance of a person.
I should like to make this distinction for the benefit of the minister and state that possibly he should rephrase it to make sure that the judge and jury, who are the court in this case and who would have to make this finding of fact, would have the knowledge that they did find this after hearing the evidence. If this fact is not reasonably established they can refer to the appearance of the accused because there is a difference between appearing to a court if the theft is over $100, which is determined without any relationship whatsoever to the appearance of the person accused of that theft.
I feel in a sense it is a different proposition to place in a statute "if it appears to the court that the person was under 18 when he committed the offence", which on many occasions would have to be determined by the physical appearance of the accused, which is not necessary if the theft is over $100. For that reason I think the statute could be made clearer. I do not say that no judge or no jury could construe the words "appears to the court" in the sense that the minister has indicated they oftentimes are construed. But it seems to me that certainly some effort should be made to make that distinction clearer in this case so that no one would make an argument based solely on the fact that if the person appears to be under 18, no matter whether the crown proves that he is 18.
What would be the interpretation of a jury if the man has a certificate, or the crown produces a birth certificate indicating that he is over 18 when he looks like a 14-year-old? Surely the lawyer is entitled to say that this boy appears, and appeared at the time of the commission of the offence, to be under 18. Why should you defeat that exemption by simply saying that he is 18? If a person is in fact proven to be 18 he can be sentenced to capital punishment and if he appears to be under 18 he should be exempt. I think this is most pertinent under the circumstances and I believe the minister should pay some attention to the remarks made by the two hon. members and not create a section wherein proof by the crown of the actual fact is excluded.
I should also like to make certain remarks concerning an accused whose mental capacity can reasonably be established to the satisfaction of the jury to be that of a person under the age of 18. It seems to me that guilt does not attach to a birth certificate-the

age of the accused-as much as it attaches to the capacity of the person who committed the crime. If we are going to exempt people under 18 from punishment by death, I feel that the minister should be able to find a way to exempt those people as to whom it has been reasonably established that their mental age is that of a person under the age of 18. In my view that is a better criterion of the guilt of the person who committed the crime of murder than a birth certificate is. A person with a birth certificate indicating an age of 17 might have the mental capacity of a person of 25 but he would be exempt from capital punishment whereas an accused 22 years old might have the mental capacity of a person of 12 or 14 but could not receive the exemption granted to the other accused. Therefore I think it is only fair that the minister should see fit to add after the provision respecting proof of age the words "or has the mental capacity of a person less than 18 years".

The question the hon. member
has asked seems to me to relate to the general question of the effect of a sentence of life imprisonment for murder or the commutation of a sentence of death to life imprisonment. The regulations of the parole board now provide that in the case of a sentence of life imprisonment there shall ordinarily be no parole before seven years have been served. Similarly, they provide that when a sentence of death is commuted to life imprisonment there shall ordinarily be no parole until ten years have actually been served. I want to make it clear that there are minimum periods. It does not mean there will be parole at the end of seven or ten years respectively.

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY

At the moment they are in the regulations which are approved by the governor in council. As I was saying, this does not mean that parole is automatic at the end of seven or ten years respectively. Parliament has entrusted to the parole board, however, the determination of whether or when a man is qualified and fit to be paroled. The other point that it is important to bear in mind in this discussion is that when a man is paroled who has been serving a sentence of life imprisonment, whether imposed by the court or as the result of commutation of the death sentence, that is his sentence. His sentence is life and if he is paroled he is under the supervision of the parole board for the balance of the sentence.
Therefore the impression should not be allowed to go abroad that when paroled, perhaps after the end of seven or ten years only, these persons are not subject to supervision, that they are completely free and that they would be liable therefore to go off, and fall into bad habits again and revert to those circumstances which led to their first crime. They are under the supervision of the parole board. There has to be a nice balance in these cases because, since the object of parole as well as the object of other portions of our reform program is to rehabilitate, one must

No, Mr. Chairman, this provision relates only to part XX of the code. Its application is only with respect to the provisions of part XX. A sentence of life imprisonment cannot be suspended, changed to probation or changed to a term of years. It is a sentence of life imprisonment but

the Parole Act provides that anyone serving a term of imprisonment, and this is a term of imprisonment, may be released from the institution >and serve the balance of his term outside the institution on the authority of the parole board.

Is there any conflict with section 656 of the code, which provides for the commutation of a sentence? The section reads:
The governor in council may commute a sentence of death to imprisonment in the penitentiary for life, or for any term of years not less than two years, or to imprisonment in a prison other than a penitentiary for a period of less than two years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman, because the only case in which the governor in council can commute is a sentence of death. This is a case where there has not been a sentence of life imprisonment imposed, but the sentence of the court is a sentence of death. Then, if the governor in council commutes it he may, as my hon. friend points out, commute it to any one of a number of different sentences. The universal practice, however, so far as I know is to commute it to a term of life imprisonment.
Certainly, now that we have a parole board it would always be the case that it would be made life imprisonment because then the parole board determines, in accordance with well worked out principles, where and when he is eligible for release from the institution so that he may serve the balance of his term outside under supervision.

I have here the Parole Act of 1958, section 6, subsection (1), of which reads as follows:
The board shall at the times prescribed by the regulations
(a) review the case of every inmate serving a sentence of imprisonment of two years or more, whether or not an application has been made by or on behalf of the inmate,-
Now, if I am not mistaken, when this act was before this parliament, there was no such minimum sentence as imprisonment for life. Therefore this type of sentence we are now considering was not contemplated when section 6 of the Parole Act was enacted. It is for this reason I asked the minister the last question, and I am still not clear about his answer. It is true that the clause before us refers to part XX of the code in so far as it relates to imprisonment and deals with where the imprisonment will be carried out, either in a penitentiary or a common prison or part in one and part in the other. Right now, I do not see anything in sections 633, 634 or 635 of the code, apart from probation, that did exist before we enacted the Parole

Act. Right now, if a man is on probation under the Parole Act, it is, as a matter of fact, a ticket of leave and he is supervised by social workers.
May I call it 10.30, Mr. Chairman?
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
On Saturday the house
leader announced a long list of items of legislation but said nothing about the estimates for the rest of the week. I wonder if we might get some indication of what we will take up tomorrow and Wednesday, and also the departments which we will consider during the rest of the week?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The intention is to carry on with legislation tomorrow, commencing with Bill No. C-92 on which fair progress has been made. The Minister of Justice has to leave sometime in the afternoon and perhaps before his departure the house would be able to complete consideration of Bill No. C-92. However, if we have not reached the other bill, No. C-97, to amend the Combines Investigation Act and Criminal Code, and the resolution dealing with the Exchequer Court Act, we will have to postpone those; but retaining the same order that I announced
Business of the House
on Saturday, the fourth item will be Bill No. C-77 concerning the rehabilitation of agricultural lands, etc., the fifth item will be Bill No. C-93, an act to amend the Freight Rates Reduction Act, and as a sixth item we will have the bill which received first reading today, to amend the Food and Drugs Act.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I at this point indicate to the house leader that the Minister of Transport will be engaged in the committee on the Canada Shipping Act tomorrow afternoon, where he was detained for the greater part of today. I do not know how he is going to be in that committee and deal with the Freight Rates Reduction Act as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
We may not reach the Freight Rates Reduction Act until the evening, after the supper hour.
The progress made tomorrow will determine what we do on Wednesday. I should like to hold open whether or not we continue with legislation. On Thursday, Friday and Saturday we will be dealing with estimates in this order, mines and technical surveys, Secretary of State, fisheries and public works.
At 10.35 p.m. the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to special order.

Tuesday, May 30, 1961
